exact_task.problem:
On X=CP1xCP1 take L=O(1,1) with product Fubini--Study metric h and closed theta=c1(L,h), using dd^c=(i/(2 pi))partial barpartial. In homogeneous coordinates (Z_i:T_i) define the genuine theta-psh singularity psi=max(log|T1T2|_h^2,log|Z1Z2|_h^2). In the dense torus x_i=log|z_i|^2, z_i=Z_i/T_i, it is max(0,x1+x2)-log(1+exp x1)-log(1+exp x2); its fixed pole points are (0,infinity) and (infinity,0). On every holomorphic frame, v+phi_h is a genuine plurisubharmonic function with its canonical upper representative and submean property, not merely an upper-semicontinuous representative of a positive-curvature distribution. The multiplier ideal I(t v) consists locally of holomorphic germs f with |f|^2 exp(-t v) integrable. Define v<=_I psi by I(tv) contained in I(t psi) for every real t>0. For a continuous obstacle on a compact K the ideal envelope is the USC regularized supremum of all theta-psh v with that ideal constraint and v<=w quasi-everywhere on K. Ordinary bounded-above type means v<=psi+C_v for a finite constant. Do not assume these competitor classes coincide.

notes.summary: The actual local ideals are I(tψ)=m_p^{max(0,floor(t)-1)} at each pole. For every genuinely θ-psh, possibly non-toric v, v≤_Iψ iff v≤ψ+C. A local weighted L²-extension argument detects the logarithmic pole with coefficient 1. All such global v moreover factor through the pencil [T1T2:Z1Z2]. Consequently ideal and ordinary envelopes agree for every smooth obstacle on all X (indeed for every common obstacle problem).
notes.detailedSummary: Near either pole, ψ equals log max(|u|²,|v|²) plus a smooth function. Radial integration gives I(tψ)=m^{max(0,floor(t)-1)}. If I(t v) is contained in these ideals for all t, weighted point L² extension, followed by a holomorphic vanishing-order estimate, gives local bounds φ≤((floor(t)-1)/t)log|z|²+C_t for the genuine psh local potential φ. Convexity of its radial maximum upgrades the limiting coefficient to the endpoint bound φ≤log|z|²+C; hence v≤ψ+C globally. The converse follows directly from integrability. The sole non-elementary analytic input is the explicitly stated, standard Ohsawa–Takegoshi hyperplane extension theorem, iterated to a point; its weight is exp(-Φ), and it is applied with Φ=tφ, not 2tφ. For factorization, a generic smooth (1,1) pencil curve has θ-degree 2 and contains both poles. Restrictions of v have atom masses at least 1 at each pole, exhausting degree 2, so v-ψ is constant on every non-identically-infinite generic fiber. Fubini and canonical psh representatives then give v=ψ_FS+u∘F globally, where ψ_FS=log(|T1T2|_h²+|Z1Z2|_h²), F=[T1T2:Z1Z2] off the poles, and u is ω_FS-psh on CP1. This proves the non-toric identification rather than assuming toric competitors.
notes.text:
Let p=(0,∞), q=(∞,0). All logarithms below are logarithms of squared absolute values when applied to coordinates, and dd^c=(i/(2π))∂bar∂ as in the question. In particular dd^c log|ζ|²=δ_0 in one complex dimension, and each Fubini–Study factor has integral 1.

1. Exact local multiplier ideals.
Near p use u=z1 and v=1/z2 and the holomorphic frame T1 Z2 for L. Its metric potential is log(1+|u|²)+log(1+|v|²), while the two sections defining ψ are represented by v and u. Thus
 ψ=log max(|u|²,|v|²)-log(1+|u|²)-log(1+|v|²).
The analogous statement holds at q. Away from p,q, ψ is locally bounded and its multiplier ideals are the full structure sheaf.

The weights max(|u|²,|v|²)^(-t) and (|u|²+|v|²)^(-t) are comparable for fixed t. If a nonzero holomorphic germ f has vanishing order k, its leading homogeneous term, or its spherical L² average, shows that the local integral has the same integrability threshold as
 ∫_0^ε r^{2k-2t+3}dr.
It is finite exactly when k+2>t. At equality the radial integral diverges logarithmically. Consequently
 I(tψ)_p=m_p^{k(t)}, I(tψ)_q=m_q^{k(t)},
 k(t)=max(0,floor(t)-1), t>0.
This includes integer t; in particular I(mψ) has order m-1 at each pole for every integer m≥1.

2. The local analytic input and recovery of the endpoint logarithmic bound.
The standard weighted L²-extension theorem is used only in the following form. If B is a bounded Euclidean ball in C^n, Φ is genuinely plurisubharmonic on B, and a is an interior point with Φ(a)>-∞, there is a holomorphic F on B with F(a)=1 and
 ∫_B |F|² exp(-Φ)dV ≤ C exp(-Φ(a)),
where C can be chosen uniformly for a in a smaller concentric ball, and is independent of Φ. No optimal value of C is required.

This is the point version obtained by iterating the hyperplane extension theorem: on a bounded pseudoconvex domain, a weighted-square-integrable holomorphic function on an affine complex hyperplane extends with its exp(-Φ) norm bounded by a constant depending only on the bounded domain in the normal direction. Apply that theorem successively to affine subspaces through a, starting from the point (whose weighted norm is exp(-Φ(a))). Each intersection with B is a ball and hence pseudoconvex; all normal diameters are bounded. This checks the domain, weight, and singular-weight hypotheses used here. The primary standard analytic input is Ohsawa–Takegoshi, “On the extension of L² holomorphic functions,” Math. Z. 195 (1987), 197–204, in its hyperplane formulation. The argument below is independent of Bergman approximation, valuative multiplier-ideal, or envelope-convergence theorems. The relevant normalization is the theorem with exp(-Φ); here Φ=tφ, exactly matching the question's exp(-t v).

Here is the consequence, with its proof. Suppose φ is genuinely psh on B centered at 0 and every germ in I(tφ)_0 vanishes to order at least k. Let H_t consist of holomorphic functions on B with finite norm ∫_B|f|²exp(-tφ). Every member of H_t has the indicated vanishing at 0. Since φ is bounded above on a slightly smaller ball, the weighted norm controls the ordinary holomorphic L² norm there. Cauchy estimates, or the Taylor remainder formula after the first k-1 jets vanish, give on a still smaller ball
 |f(z)|² ≤ A_{t,k}|z|^{2k} ||f||_{H_t}².
One can first shrink B so that φ is bounded above on its closure; the extension theorem is then applied on this shrunk ball. For φ(z)>-∞ apply point extension to Φ=tφ and obtain f_z(z)=1 with norm at most C exp(-tφ(z)). Substitution gives
 exp(tφ(z))≤C A_{t,k}|z|^{2k},
 hence
 φ(z)≤(k/t)log|z|²+C_{t,k}.
The inequality holds at points with φ=-∞ as well. If an almost-everywhere version is obtained, the canonical psh submean representative promotes it to the pointwise version away from 0.

For completeness, the endpoint in this estimate is not obtained by incorrectly demanding constants uniform in t. Let
 M(s)=sup_{|z|≤exp(s/2)}φ(z), s<s0.
The maximum on each complex line is convex in s by the subharmonic three-circles theorem; their supremum M is finite, nondecreasing, and convex. Write ν for its limiting slope as s→-∞. If φ≤c log|z|²+C, then ν≥c. Convexity also gives the endpoint estimate
 M(s)≤M(s0)+ν(s-s0), s<s0.
Indeed every secant slope ending at s0 is at least the limiting left slope ν. Therefore if ν≥1, then φ≤log|z|²+C on a neighborhood of 0. This supplies the coefficient exactly 1, not only each coefficient less than 1.

3. Equality of the full competitor classes.
Let v be any θ-psh function satisfying I(t v)⊂I(tψ) for every real t>0. On a frame near p or q put φ=v+φ_h; the hypothesis is unaffected by the smooth φ_h. Apply the preceding argument with k=k(t). The coefficients k(t)/t tend to 1. The radial convexity endpoint argument gives
 v+φ_h≤log(|u|²+|v|²)+C.
Since this logarithm differs from log max(|u|²,|v|²) by at most log 2, v≤ψ+C locally at each pole. On their complement ψ is continuous and finite, and compactness and the local upper bounds for v give a single finite global constant C_v. Thus v≤ψ+C_v on X.

Conversely, if v≤ψ+C_v, then exp(-tψ)≤exp(t C_v)exp(-t v). Every germ integrable against the latter is integrable against the former. This proves
 {v θ-psh: v≤_Iψ}={v θ-psh: v≤ψ+C_v for some finite C_v}.
No rotation invariance has been imposed anywhere. The canonical submean hypothesis in the question is used in the local extension/psh arguments; a distributional upper representative with artificial spikes would not suffice.

Because these are the identical function classes before imposing the obstacle, their obstacle-restricted classes, suprema, and USC regularizations agree for every common obstacle problem. In particular they agree for every smooth obstacle on all X, as requested. They also agree for a continuous obstacle on any compact K under the question's quasi-everywhere convention.

4. Pencil rigidity for every member of the class.
Define off p,q
 F=[T1T2:Z1Z2],
 ψ_FS=log(|T1T2|_h²+|Z1Z2|_h²).
We have ψ≤ψ_FS≤ψ+log 2. On the dense torus write Q=z1 z2, s=log|Q|² and φ_X=log(1+exp x1)+log(1+exp x2); then
 ψ_FS=log(1+exp s)-φ_X.

For Q∈C*, the closure C_Q={Z1Z2=Q T1T2} is a smooth rational (1,1) curve, containing p and q. The θ-degree of C_Q is 2. Except for those fibers on which the restriction of v is identically -∞, the restriction is a genuine θ|C_Q-psh function. The bound v≤ψ+C forces an atom of mass at least 1 at each p,q: in a local parameter on C_Q, ψ=log|ζ|²+O(1). The total mass of θ|C_Q+dd^c(v|C_Q) is 2 by Stokes, so this current is exactly δ_p+δ_q. Also θ|C_Q+dd^c(ψ|C_Q)=δ_p+δ_q, since T1T2 restricts to a section with precisely those two simple zeros and Q is constant on the fiber. Thus v-ψ is distributionally harmonic on the compact C_Q and is constant. Equivalently v+φ_X is constant on the torus part of C_Q.

Fubini in the holomorphic torus coordinates (z1,Q) shows that almost every such fiber has non-identically-infinite restriction. Let S={z1=1}, identified with CP1 by Q=z2. For those generic fibers, their constant is attained at S and is finite. Consequently the restriction v|S is not identically -∞. Put
 u=v|S+log 2.
It is an ω_FS-psh function on CP1, since θ|S=ω_FS. Notice ψ_FS|S=-log 2. The fiber calculation now says, almost everywhere on the torus,
 v=ψ_FS+u∘F.
Both sides have genuine psh local potentials and their canonical representatives are determined by their almost-everywhere values. Thus this equality holds everywhere off p,q. The right side has the canonical global extension with value -∞ at p,q: u has a finite upper bound on compact CP1, and ψ_FS has the indicated logarithmic poles. Both sides therefore agree on all X.

Conversely, for any non-identically-infinite ω_FS-psh u, ψ_FS+u∘F is θ-psh off p,q (its curvature there is F*(ω_FS+dd^c u)). In a frame its potential is bounded above by log(|a|²+|b|²)+C, where a,b are the two pencil sections. The psh removable-extension theorem across their isolated common zeros gives the canonical global extension, with value -∞ there. It is bounded above by ψ+C and hence belongs to both classes. This proves the complete possibly non-toric pencil description. On the torus it can be written
 v=χ(Q)-φ_X,
 where χ=log(1+|Q|²)+u is subharmonic in the affine base coordinate and χ(Q)≤max(0,log|Q|²)+C.

correctness.report:
The argument establishes the note's claims, conditional on the standard analytic inputs listed below. Radial integration gives the stated multiplier ideals, including the integer thresholds. The extension argument uses precisely the weight exp(-tφ); vanishing jets then give the coefficient k(t)/t. Convexity of the radial maximum correctly supplies the endpoint coefficient 1 without requiring constants uniform in t. This proves equality of the full competitor classes without a toric assumption.

The pencil argument also checks out: each smooth nonzero finite fiber has degree 2, and the two forced unit atoms exhaust its curvature measure. Fubini supplies almost-everywhere good fibers; restriction to the transverse section identifies the base potential; equality of canonical psh representatives extends the resulting almost-everywhere identity. The removable extension at the two base points has value -∞. Both summaries accurately describe these conclusions and dependencies. Equality for smooth global obstacles follows immediately from equality of the unrestricted classes.

premises: Weighted point L² extension, in the point form of the Ohsawa–Takegoshi theorem: Let B be a bounded Euclidean ball in C^n and B' a smaller concentric ball with closure contained in B. There is a constant C depending only on B, B', and n such that, for every plurisubharmonic function Φ on B and every a in B' with Φ(a)>−∞, there is F holomorphic on B satisfying F(a)=1 and ∫_B |F|² exp(−Φ) dV ≤ C exp(−Φ(a)). The constant is independent of Φ and a, and singular plurisubharmonic weights are permitted. The weight convention is exp(−Φ).

Plurisubharmonic radial three-circles theorem: If φ is a non-identically−∞ plurisubharmonic function on B(0,R) in C^n, then M(s)=sup_{|z|≤exp(s/2)} φ(z) is finite, nondecreasing, and convex for s<2 log R.

Restriction and uniqueness properties of canonical plurisubharmonic functions: If φ is plurisubharmonic on a complex manifold and G is a holomorphic map from a connected complex manifold into its domain, then φ∘G is plurisubharmonic or identically −∞. A non-identically−∞ plurisubharmonic function is locally integrable, and two canonical plurisubharmonic functions that agree almost everywhere agree everywhere.

Logarithmic bounds and curvature mass on a compact Riemann surface: Let C be a compact connected Riemann surface, let ω be a smooth real closed (1,1)-form, and let u be a non-identically−∞ function whose canonical local potentials relative to ω are subharmonic. With dd^c=(i/(2π))∂bar∂, the positive measure μ=ω+dd^c u has total mass ∫_C ω. If, in a local coordinate ζ centered at a, u(ζ)≤c log|ζ|²+O(1) for c≥0, then μ({a})≥c.

Poincaré–Lelong formula with squared norms: For a nonzero holomorphic section s of a smoothly Hermitian holomorphic line bundle (E,h) on a complex manifold, with c1(E,h)=dd^c φ_h in a holomorphic frame whose squared norm is exp(−φ_h), and dd^c=(i/(2π))∂bar∂, one has dd^c log|s|_h²=[div(s)]−c1(E,h) as currents. In one complex dimension, dd^c log|ζ|²=δ_0.

Removable extension for plurisubharmonic functions: Let A be a proper analytic subset of a complex manifold Ω. If φ is plurisubharmonic on Ω\A and locally bounded above near A, its canonical upper extension, defined at A by the limit superior from Ω\A, is plurisubharmonic on Ω.

nondependency_literature_notes.text:
Inspected source: [Demailly, Complex Analytic and Differential Geometry](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~demarco/Math274/Demailly_ComplexAnalyticDiffGeom.pdf), Chapter I; printed and PDF page numbers coincide here.

I.4.17, p.35: “If Ω is connected”, a subharmonic u is either identically −∞ or locally integrable. I.5.3, p.39, includes psh functions among subharmonic functions. On disconnected sets, require nontriviality on every component.

I.5.5, p.39, assumes precisely that componentwise nontriviality; radial convolutions are smooth psh and decrease pointwise to u as their radii decrease to zero. I.5.8, p.40, supplies the unique locally integrable psh representative of a distribution with positive complex Hessian.

I.5.22, p.44, defines pluripolarity using connected local neighborhoods and non-identically−∞ psh witnesses. I.5.24, p.45, extends v∈Psh(X\A) uniquely across a closed pluripolar A when v is “locally bounded above near A”. It assumes no global connectedness. I.5.26, p.45, states that X\A is connected when X is connected.

Thus global nontriviality alone on a disconnected space does not justify local integrability.

nondependency_literature_notes.text:
Inspected primary full text: [Bo Berndtsson, The extension theorem of Ohsawa–Takegoshi and the theorem of Donnelly–Fefferman, Ann. Inst. Fourier 46 (1996), 1083–1094](https://www.numdam.org/article/AIF_1996__46_4_1083_0.pdf).

Theorem A, printed p.1083 (PDF p.2), concerns a bounded pseudoconvex domain D⊂C^k, a plurisubharmonic φ, and a complex hyperplane H. For holomorphic f on D∩H with finite weighted norm, it provides a holomorphic extension F satisfying
∫_D |F|²e^(−φ)dV_k ≤ C_D ∫_(D∩H) |f|²e^(−φ)dV_(k−1).
The constant “depends only on the diameter” of D. These are Euclidean ambient and induced slice volumes.

The theorem imposes neither smoothness nor boundedness of φ, and no boundary regularity. The smooth-weight, smoothly bounded strictly pseudoconvex setting on p.1086 (PDF p.5) is a proof reduction. The conclusion on p.1088 (PDF p.7) gives C_D=4π when D⊂{|z₁|<1}. Translation and unitary coordinates permit affine hyperplanes.

The exponent is e^(−φ), with no implicit factor two.

nondependency_literature_notes.summary: The hyperplane theorem legitimately yields the requested point estimate, including singular weights, uniformly in a; a valid nonoptimal constant is (16πR²)^n for a radius-R ball.
nondependency_literature_notes.detailedSummary: An affine flag through a consists of connected pseudoconvex ball slices. Transverse scaling costs (2R)² per extension, giving F(a)=1 and ∫_B|F|²e^(−Φ)≤(16πR²)^n e^(−Φ(a)). A separate exhaustion, convolution, Montel, and Fatou argument verifies the singular-weight passage and its dependence on canonical point values.
nondependency_literature_notes.text:
The following is an independent derivation from the inspected hyperplane theorem in n2 and the psh facts in n1.

Let B=B(c,R)⊂C^n, let Φ be genuine psh on B, and assume Φ(a)>−∞. Then there exists F∈O(B) with F(a)=1 and
∫_B |F|²e^(−Φ)dV ≤ (16πR²)^n e^(−Φ(a)).
The constant is independent of Φ and a. Consequently it is uniform on any fixed smaller concentric ball; this derivation actually works uniformly for all a∈B. No sharp constant is claimed.

First suppose Φ is smooth. Define E_k={z_(k+1)=a_(k+1),…,z_n=a_n} and D_k=B∩E_k, for 0≤k≤n. Thus D_0={a} and D_n=B. Each positive-dimensional D_k is a nonempty connected Euclidean ball in its affine complex space, hence bounded and pseudoconvex. Moreover D_(k−1) is a hyperplane section of D_k. Every coordinate satisfies |z_j−a_j|<2R on B.

Starting with f_0(a)=1, extend f_(k−1) from D_(k−1) to D_k. Identify E_k with C^k using orthonormal coordinates and scale y=(z−a)/(2R). The transverse coordinate has modulus less than one. Berndtsson’s estimate therefore applies with constant 4π in the scaled coordinates. Ambient and slice volumes scale by (2R)^(2k) and (2R)^(2k−2), respectively, so after scaling back,
∫_(D_k)|f_k|²e^(−Φ)dV_k ≤ 4π(2R)² ∫_(D_(k−1))|f_(k−1)|²e^(−Φ)dV_(k−1).
For k=1, the hyperplane is the point a; zero-dimensional Euclidean volume gives it mass one. The theorem has no exclusion of this dimension. Multiplying these n estimates proves the assertion for F=f_n.

The flag also legitimizes direct iteration for a singular weight: restriction of genuine psh to an affine complex subspace is psh, and every slice contains the finite-valued point a. Thus no restriction is identically −∞. Connectedness and n1 give local integrability on every positive-dimensional slice. Each extension supplies the finite norm needed by the next step. This avoids any unjustified assumption that arbitrary hyperplane restrictions of a singular weight must be nontrivial.

For completeness, singular weights can instead be handled independently from the smooth case. Exhaust B by concentric balls B_j containing a, with radii increasing to R. Choose radial convolution radii ε_j decreasing to zero, small enough that Φ_j=Φ*ρ_(ε_j) is defined and smooth psh on a neighborhood of the closure of B_j. Canonicality gives Φ_j(a)→Φ(a), and the submean property gives Φ_j(a)≥Φ(a). Apply the smooth construction on B_j, using the same upper radius R, obtaining F_j(a)=1 and
∫_(B_j)|F_j|²e^(−Φ_j) ≤ (16πR²)^n e^(−Φ(a)).
On each relatively compact subdomain, Φ_j has a common finite upper bound. The displayed estimate therefore bounds the ordinary local L² norms of F_j. Holomorphic submean estimates and Montel’s theorem give a subsequence converging locally uniformly to F∈O(B), with F(a)=1. Since Φ_j→Φ pointwise and Φ is finite almost everywhere, Fatou’s lemma on each fixed exhaustion ball, followed by monotone exhaustion, gives the asserted weighted estimate on B.

For the task’s multiplier-ideal convention, the input weight is Φ=t times the genuine local psh potential, so the exponent is exactly e^(−t·potential). If another source writes e^(−2ϕ), substitute ϕ=Φ/2. The choice of dd^c normalization does not alter this exponent or psh positivity. Replacing a local potential v+φ_h by v changes integrability only by a smooth positive factor.

Canonicality is essential. The usc function equal to M>0 at the center of B and zero elsewhere represents the zero distribution, but is not genuine psh. For F(center)=1, the holomorphic submean inequality gives ∫_B|F|²≥Vol(B), contradicting a weight-independent bound C e^(−M) as M→∞.

Finally, the removable extension in n1 has values ṽ(a)=limsup_(z→a,z∉A)v(z) at a∈A. This follows from upper semicontinuity and the ball submean inequality because pluripolar A has measure zero. The extension statement itself is local; connectedness is needed only when invoking nontriviality-to-integrability or connectedness of the complement. These observations close the identified analytic-source gaps without asserting any envelope-convergence theorem.

All three supplied premises are standalone mathematical claims and are established in their stated scope. Berndtsson’s primary paper proves the weighted hyperplane extension theorem with exp(−Φ) and a constant controlled solely by domain diameter. Translation, unitary coordinates and scaling give the asserted uniform constant for balls of radius at most R, including affine hyperplanes and the one-dimensional point case. The note’s successive restrictions are nontrivial because the weight is finite at the extension point. [Source](https://www.numdam.org/item/10.5802/aif.1541.pdf)

Demailly’s logarithmic-slope formula establishes premise 1 with the exact normalization: apply the source’s operator (i/π)∂∂̄ to u=g/2. This equals the note’s dd^c g; in one complex dimension its Lelong number is its atom mass. The note applies this only to nontrivial subharmonic curve restrictions. [Source](https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/manuscripts/analmeth_book.pdf)

Harvey–Lawson’s Theorem 8.1, specialized to its first branch Λ^C_1=P^C, establishes premise 2 for closed locally pluripolar sets, hence for proper analytic subsets. Equation (3.1) gives exactly the stated limsup extension. The converse pencil construction satisfies the required local upper bound, and its logarithmic bound forces extension value −∞ at both base points. [Source](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1303.0437)

This verdict approves the external premises and their applications; it does not assess completion of the larger kernel-convergence task.

passages.statement: Weighted holomorphic hyperplane extension on Euclidean balls (Ohsawa–Takegoshi): For every integer n≥1 and R>0 there is a constant C(n,R) such that the following holds. Let B⊂C^n be a Euclidean ball of radius at most R, let H be an affine complex hyperplane meeting B, and let Φ be a genuine plurisubharmonic function on B whose restriction to B∩H is not identically −∞. Every holomorphic f on B∩H with finite integral ∫_{B∩H}|f|² exp(−Φ)dλ_H has a holomorphic extension F on B satisfying ∫_B|F|² exp(−Φ)dλ≤C(n,R)∫_{B∩H}|f|² exp(−Φ)dλ_H. The constant is independent of Φ, f, and the position of H. For n=1, H is a point and its zero-dimensional measure is one.

failed_original_notes.text:
Let p=(0,∞), q=(∞,0). All logarithms below are logarithms of squared absolute values when applied to coordinates, and dd^c=(i/(2π))∂bar∂ as in the question. In particular dd^c log|ζ|²=δ_0 in one complex dimension, and each Fubini–Study factor has integral 1.

1. Exact local multiplier ideals.
Near p use u=z1 and v=1/z2 and the holomorphic frame T1 Z2 for L. Its metric potential is log(1+|u|²)+log(1+|v|²), while the two sections defining ψ are represented by v and u. Thus
 ψ=log max(|u|²,|v|²)-log(1+|u|²)-log(1+|v|²).
The analogous statement holds at q. Away from p,q, ψ is locally bounded and its multiplier ideals are the full structure sheaf.

The weights max(|u|²,|v|²)^(-t) and (|u|²+|v|²)^(-t) are comparable for fixed t. If a nonzero holomorphic germ f has vanishing order k, its leading homogeneous term, or its spherical L² average, shows that the local integral has the same integrability threshold as
 ∫_0^ε r^{2k-2t+3}dr.
It is finite exactly when k+2>t. At equality the radial integral diverges logarithmically. Consequently
 I(tψ)_p=m_p^{k(t)}, I(tψ)_q=m_q^{k(t)},
 k(t)=max(0,floor(t)-1), t>0.
This includes integer t; in particular I(mψ) has order m-1 at each pole for every integer m≥1.

2. The local analytic input and recovery of the endpoint logarithmic bound.
The standard weighted L²-extension theorem is used only in the following form. If B is a bounded Euclidean ball in C^n, Φ is genuinely plurisubharmonic on B, and a is an interior point with Φ(a)>-∞, there is a holomorphic F on B with F(a)=1 and
 ∫_B |F|² exp(-Φ)dV ≤ C exp(-Φ(a)),
where C can be chosen uniformly for a in a smaller concentric ball, and is independent of Φ. No optimal value of C is required.

This is the point version obtained by iterating the hyperplane extension theorem: on a bounded pseudoconvex domain, a weighted-square-integrable holomorphic function on an affine complex hyperplane extends with its exp(-Φ) norm bounded by a constant depending only on the bounded domain in the normal direction. Apply that theorem successively to affine subspaces through a, starting from the point (whose weighted norm is exp(-Φ(a))). Each intersection with B is a ball and hence pseudoconvex; all normal diameters are bounded. This checks the domain, weight, and singular-weight hypotheses used here. The primary standard analytic input is Ohsawa–Takegoshi, “On the extension of L² holomorphic functions,” Math. Z. 195 (1987), 197–204, in its hyperplane formulation. The argument below is independent of Bergman approximation, valuative multiplier-ideal, or envelope-convergence theorems. The relevant normalization is the theorem with exp(-Φ); here Φ=tφ, exactly matching the question's exp(-t v).

Here is the consequence, with its proof. Suppose φ is genuinely psh on B centered at 0 and every germ in I(tφ)_0 vanishes to order at least k. Let H_t consist of holomorphic functions on B with finite norm ∫_B|f|²exp(-tφ). Every member of H_t has the indicated vanishing at 0. Since φ is bounded above on a slightly smaller ball, the weighted norm controls the ordinary holomorphic L² norm there. Cauchy estimates, or the Taylor remainder formula after the first k-1 jets vanish, give on a still smaller ball
 |f(z)|² ≤ A_{t,k}|z|^{2k} ||f||_{H_t}².
One can first shrink B so that φ is bounded above on its closure; the extension theorem is then applied on this shrunk ball. For φ(z)>-∞ apply point extension to Φ=tφ and obtain f_z(z)=1 with norm at most C exp(-tφ(z)). Substitution gives
 exp(tφ(z))≤C A_{t,k}|z|^{2k},
 hence
 φ(z)≤(k/t)log|z|²+C_{t,k}.
The inequality holds at points with φ=-∞ as well. If an almost-everywhere version is obtained, the canonical psh submean representative promotes it to the pointwise version away from 0.

For completeness, the endpoint in this estimate is not obtained by incorrectly demanding constants uniform in t. Let
 M(s)=sup_{|z|≤exp(s/2)}φ(z), s<s0.
The maximum on each complex line is convex in s by the subharmonic three-circles theorem; their supremum M is finite, nondecreasing, and convex. Write ν for its limiting slope as s→-∞. If φ≤c log|z|²+C, then ν≥c. Convexity also gives the endpoint estimate
 M(s)≤M(s0)+ν(s-s0), s<s0.
Indeed every secant slope ending at s0 is at least the limiting left slope ν. Therefore if ν≥1, then φ≤log|z|²+C on a neighborhood of 0. This supplies the coefficient exactly 1, not only each coefficient less than 1.

3. Equality of the full competitor classes.
Let v be any θ-psh function satisfying I(t v)⊂I(tψ) for every real t>0. On a frame near p or q put φ=v+φ_h; the hypothesis is unaffected by the smooth φ_h. Apply the preceding argument with k=k(t). The coefficients k(t)/t tend to 1. The radial convexity endpoint argument gives
 v+φ_h≤log(|u|²+|v|²)+C.
Since this logarithm differs from log max(|u|²,|v|²) by at most log 2, v≤ψ+C locally at each pole. On their complement ψ is continuous and finite, and compactness and the local upper bounds for v give a single finite global constant C_v. Thus v≤ψ+C_v on X.

Conversely, if v≤ψ+C_v, then exp(-tψ)≤exp(t C_v)exp(-t v). Every germ integrable against the latter is integrable against the former. This proves
 {v θ-psh: v≤_Iψ}={v θ-psh: v≤ψ+C_v for some finite C_v}.
No rotation invariance has been imposed anywhere. The canonical submean hypothesis in the question is used in the local extension/psh arguments; a distributional upper representative with artificial spikes would not suffice.

Because these are the identical function classes before imposing the obstacle, their obstacle-restricted classes, suprema, and USC regularizations agree for every common obstacle problem. In particular they agree for every smooth obstacle on all X, as requested. They also agree for a continuous obstacle on any compact K under the question's quasi-everywhere convention.

4. Pencil rigidity for every member of the class.
Define off p,q
 F=[T1T2:Z1Z2],
 ψ_FS=log(|T1T2|_h²+|Z1Z2|_h²).
We have ψ≤ψ_FS≤ψ+log 2. On the dense torus write Q=z1 z2, s=log|Q|² and φ_X=log(1+exp x1)+log(1+exp x2); then
 ψ_FS=log(1+exp s)-φ_X.

For Q∈C*, the closure C_Q={Z1Z2=Q T1T2} is a smooth rational (1,1) curve, containing p and q. The θ-degree of C_Q is 2. Except for those fibers on which the restriction of v is identically -∞, the restriction is a genuine θ|C_Q-psh function. The bound v≤ψ+C forces an atom of mass at least 1 at each p,q: in a local parameter on C_Q, ψ=log|ζ|²+O(1). The total mass of θ|C_Q+dd^c(v|C_Q) is 2 by Stokes, so this current is exactly δ_p+δ_q. Also θ|C_Q+dd^c(ψ|C_Q)=δ_p+δ_q, since T1T2 restricts to a section with precisely those two simple zeros and Q is constant on the fiber. Thus v-ψ is distributionally harmonic on the compact C_Q and is constant. Equivalently v+φ_X is constant on the torus part of C_Q.

Fubini in the holomorphic torus coordinates (z1,Q) shows that almost every such fiber has non-identically-infinite restriction. Let S={z1=1}, identified with CP1 by Q=z2. For those generic fibers, their constant is attained at S and is finite. Consequently the restriction v|S is not identically -∞. Put
 u=v|S+log 2.
It is an ω_FS-psh function on CP1, since θ|S=ω_FS. Notice ψ_FS|S=-log 2. The fiber calculation now says, almost everywhere on the torus,
 v=ψ_FS+u∘F.
Both sides have genuine psh local potentials and their canonical representatives are determined by their almost-everywhere values. Thus this equality holds everywhere off p,q. The right side has the canonical global extension with value -∞ at p,q: u has a finite upper bound on compact CP1, and ψ_FS has the indicated logarithmic poles. Both sides therefore agree on all X.

Conversely, for any non-identically-infinite ω_FS-psh u, ψ_FS+u∘F is θ-psh off p,q (its curvature there is F*(ω_FS+dd^c u)). In a frame its potential is bounded above by log(|a|²+|b|²)+C, where a,b are the two pencil sections. The psh removable-extension theorem across their isolated common zeros gives the canonical global extension, with value -∞ there. It is bounded above by ψ+C and hence belongs to both classes. This proves the complete possibly non-toric pencil description. On the torus it can be written
 v=χ(Q)-φ_X,
 where χ=log(1+|Q|²)+u is subharmonic in the affine base coordinate and χ(Q)≤max(0,log|Q|²)+C.

correctness.report:
The argument establishes the note's claims, conditional on the standard analytic inputs listed below. Radial integration gives the stated multiplier ideals, including the integer thresholds. The extension argument uses precisely the weight exp(-tφ); vanishing jets then give the coefficient k(t)/t. Convexity of the radial maximum correctly supplies the endpoint coefficient 1 without requiring constants uniform in t. This proves equality of the full competitor classes without a toric assumption.

The pencil argument also checks out: each smooth nonzero finite fiber has degree 2, and the two forced unit atoms exhaust its curvature measure. Fubini supplies almost-everywhere good fibers; restriction to the transverse section identifies the base potential; equality of canonical psh representatives extends the resulting almost-everywhere identity. The removable extension at the two base points has value -∞. Both summaries accurately describe these conclusions and dependencies. Equality for smooth global obstacles follows immediately from equality of the unrestricted classes.

premises: Weighted point L² extension, in the point form of the Ohsawa–Takegoshi theorem: Let B be a bounded Euclidean ball in C^n and B' a smaller concentric ball with closure contained in B. There is a constant C depending only on B, B', and n such that, for every plurisubharmonic function Φ on B and every a in B' with Φ(a)>−∞, there is F holomorphic on B satisfying F(a)=1 and ∫_B |F|² exp(−Φ) dV ≤ C exp(−Φ(a)). The constant is independent of Φ and a, and singular plurisubharmonic weights are permitted. The weight convention is exp(−Φ).

Plurisubharmonic radial three-circles theorem: If φ is a non-identically−∞ plurisubharmonic function on B(0,R) in C^n, then M(s)=sup_{|z|≤exp(s/2)} φ(z) is finite, nondecreasing, and convex for s<2 log R.

Restriction and uniqueness properties of canonical plurisubharmonic functions: If φ is plurisubharmonic on a complex manifold and G is a holomorphic map from a connected complex manifold into its domain, then φ∘G is plurisubharmonic or identically −∞. A non-identically−∞ plurisubharmonic function is locally integrable, and two canonical plurisubharmonic functions that agree almost everywhere agree everywhere.

Logarithmic bounds and curvature mass on a compact Riemann surface: Let C be a compact connected Riemann surface, let ω be a smooth real closed (1,1)-form, and let u be a non-identically−∞ function whose canonical local potentials relative to ω are subharmonic. With dd^c=(i/(2π))∂bar∂, the positive measure μ=ω+dd^c u has total mass ∫_C ω. If, in a local coordinate ζ centered at a, u(ζ)≤c log|ζ|²+O(1) for c≥0, then μ({a})≥c.

Poincaré–Lelong formula with squared norms: For a nonzero holomorphic section s of a smoothly Hermitian holomorphic line bundle (E,h) on a complex manifold, with c1(E,h)=dd^c φ_h in a holomorphic frame whose squared norm is exp(−φ_h), and dd^c=(i/(2π))∂bar∂, one has dd^c log|s|_h²=[div(s)]−c1(E,h) as currents. In one complex dimension, dd^c log|ζ|²=δ_0.

Removable extension for plurisubharmonic functions: Let A be a proper analytic subset of a complex manifold Ω. If φ is plurisubharmonic on Ω\A and locally bounded above near A, its canonical upper extension, defined at A by the limit superior from Ω\A, is plurisubharmonic on Ω.

failed_original_notes.summary: The actual spaces are exactly span{s_ab:0≤a,b≤m, |a-b|≤1}, with dim V_m=3m+1 and growth exponent 1. These families are not multiplicative; the diagonal ordinary-section subseries alone has dim m+1 and is not the actual ideal selection. All monomials are orthogonal, their norms are explicit truncated Gaussian products, and the normalized weighted trace measure tends to dt on x1=x2=t∈[0,1] times independent angular Haar. failed_original_notes.detailedSummary: Using the integer ideal order m-1 at both poles, a monomial has local orders a+m-b and b+m-a, giving exactly |a-b|≤1; no cancellation changes these coefficientwise conditions. Thus V_m has 3m+1 elements in its monomial basis, while V_0=C. In the original norm, φ_X cancels w's metric part, and ||s_ab||²=(1/9) I_m(a/m) I_m(b/m), with I_m(p)=∫_{-1}^2 exp(m(px-x²/2))dx. Uniformly p∈[0,1], I_m(p)=exp(mp²/2) sqrt(2π/m)(1+O(m^{-1/2}exp(-m/2))). The normalized kernel trace measure (3m+1)^{-1} B_m exp(-mw)ν is the average of 3m+1 product truncated Gaussian distributions centered at (a/m,b/m), times angular Haar. Their uniform concentration and three elementary Riemann sums give the diagonal t∈[0,1] limit. Although the growth exponent is 1, the associated rational maps can have two-dimensional image: this is not a multiplicative graded section ring, and Iitaka assertions for such rings are inapplicable.
failed_original_notes.text:
Use the local ideal computation of n1. For m≥1 define
 s_ab=Z1^a T1^{m-a} Z2^b T2^{m-b}, 0≤a,b≤m.
At p=(0,∞), in the frame T1^m Z2^m this section is u^a v^{m-b}, so its vanishing order is a+m-b. At q its vanishing order is b+m-a. The required orders for I(mψ) are m-1. Thus the two inequalities are exactly
 a-b≥-1, a-b≤1.
A general section is the sum of these distinct local monomials. Terms of insufficient degree cannot cancel identically, since their exponent pairs are distinct. Therefore the complete actual space is
 V_m=span{s_ab:0≤a,b≤m, |a-b|≤1}.
There are m+1 diagonal terms and m terms on each neighboring diagonal, giving
 N_m=dim V_m=3m+1.
With the natural convention V_0=C, the dimension statement also gives N_0=1. The intrinsic Hilbert growth exponent is 1, with N_m/m→3.

One must not replace this by the diagonal family. The sections whose individual logarithmic potentials (1/m)log|s|_h² have the ordinary bounded-above type must vanish to order at least m at both poles; they have a=b and form a space of dimension m+1. Despite equality of the full θ-psh competitor classes in n1, this is not the multiplier-ideal selection at the single exponent m. Also the actual V_m are not multiplicative: offsets 1 multiplied by offsets 1 give offset 2. For example a nonzero offset-1 element of V_1 has square outside V_2. Consequently the usual graded-section-ring/Iitaka interpretation of growth cannot be silently applied. In fact the rational maps from V_m have two-dimensional image on the torus, since ratios of suitable sections recover z1 and z2. The normalization relevant to the actual Hilbert spaces is N_m=3m+1, not an ambient m² normalization and not m+1.

Here are exact norms in the problem's original Hilbert structure. Put
 φ_X(x)=log(1+exp x1)+log(1+exp x2),
 Q(x)=(x1²+x2²)/2,
 w=Q-φ_X.
On the torus,
 |s_ab|_h^2=exp(a x1+b x2-mφ_X).
Integration over independent normalized angular Haar makes these monomials orthogonal. Define
 I_m(p)=∫_{-1}^2 exp(m(px-x²/2))dx,
 J_m(p)=∫_{-1}^2 exp(-m(x-p)²/2)dx.
Then for p=a/m, r=b/m,
 A_m(a,b):=||s_ab||²=(1/9)I_m(p)I_m(r)
 =(1/9)exp(m(p²+r²)/2)J_m(p)J_m(r).
The normalized monomials s_ab/sqrt(A_m(a,b)) are an orthonormal basis of the entire actual V_m. Hence
 B_m(x)=exp(-mφ_X(x)) Σ_{0≤a,b≤m, |a-b|≤1} exp(a x1+b x2)/A_m(a,b).
This is angularly invariant. These formulas retain the original Hilbert norm rather than replacing it with an asymptotic model.

Every center p∈[0,1] has distance at least 1 from both endpoints of [-1,2]. Gaussian tail bounds therefore give, uniformly for such p,
 J_m(p)=sqrt(2π/m)(1+O(m^{-1/2}exp(-m/2))),
 I_m(p)=exp(mp²/2)sqrt(2π/m)(1+O(m^{-1/2}exp(-m/2))).
For example each missing tail is bounded by exp(-m/2)/m, whereas the full integral is sqrt(2π/m). Independently of this asymptotic, useful global inequalities are
 c/sqrt(m)≤J_m(p)≤sqrt(2π/m)
 for all m≥1 and p∈[0,1], where c=∫_{-1}^1 exp(-y²/2)dy works by scaling. Thus
 c²/(9m) exp((a²+b²)/(2m))≤A_m(a,b)≤2π/(9m) exp((a²+b²)/(2m)).

Define the normalized kernel trace probability measure on K by
 μ_m=(1/N_m)B_m exp(-mw)ν.
The factor exp(-mw) is essential: this is the weighted measure associated with the stated Hilbert norm, and its total mass is exactly 1. By the exact norm formula, the contribution of the (a,b) basis element is the probability density
 [exp(-m(x1-a/m)²/2)/J_m(a/m)]
 ×[exp(-m(x2-b/m)²/2)/J_m(b/m)] dx1 dx2
 ×dθ1/(2π) dθ2/(2π),
 restricted to D=[-1,2]^2. Thus μ_m is the arithmetic average of these N_m product Gaussian probabilities.

For any fixed ε>0 their mass outside the ε-neighborhood of the center tends to zero uniformly in all selected a,b. Uniform continuity of a test function on K consequently reduces its μ_m integral to the arithmetic average of its angularly averaged values at (a/m,b/m), up to a term tending uniformly to zero. The diagonal sum has m+1 points (j/m,j/m). The two neighboring sums have m points (j/m,(j+1)/m) and ((j+1)/m,j/m). All three Riemann sums tend to the same integral over t∈[0,1], and (m+1)/(3m+1), m/(3m+1), m/(3m+1) tend to 1/3. Therefore, weakly on X,
 μ_m → μ,
 ∫_X f dμ=∫_0^1∫_{[0,2π]^2} f(z1=exp(t/2+iθ1), z2=exp(t/2+iθ2)) dθ1/(2π)dθ2/(2π)dt.
The support is the real diagonal x1=x2=t, 0≤t≤1, with both independent angles. If instead the trace measure is divided by m, its limit is 3μ and its total mass tends to 3. Dividing by the ambient m² gives zero. These statements supply both the probability and intrinsic-growth normalizations.

This note, together with n1 and n2, is a complete solution of the exact ideal-selected task. In particular it uses the whole multiplier-ideal competitor class, not a replacement diagonal monomial series.

1. Identification of the full envelope.
Write φ_X(x)=log(1+exp x1)+log(1+exp x2), Q(x)=(x1²+x2²)/2, and s=x1+x2. Define
 g(s)=sup_{0≤p≤1}(ps-p²)
 =0 if s≤0;
 =s²/4 if 0≤s≤2;
 =s-1 if s≥2.
The answer on the torus is
 P(x)=g(x1+x2)-φ_X(x).
There is its canonical global θ-psh extension; in particular P(p)=P(q)=-∞.

First prove that every full ideal competitor is at most P. By n1 it is of the form
 v=χ(z1z2)-φ_X,
 where χ is subharmonic in the affine base coordinate, and χ(Q_base)≤max(0,log|Q_base|²)+C globally on C*. This representation permits arbitrary angular dependence of χ, so it has not presumed toric v.

On the open interior Ω of K, the quasi-everywhere obstacle inequality implies an almost-everywhere inequality, since pluripolar sets have zero Euclidean volume. In a torus frame the genuine psh potential v+φ_X therefore satisfies v+φ_X≤Q almost everywhere on Ω. Its canonical submean property, and continuity of Q, imply the same inequality at every point of Ω: average over balls shrinking to a point. At a base point with log|Q_base|²=s∈(-2,4), take x1=x2=s/2 and choose angles with the prescribed product. This gives
 χ(Q_base)≤s²/4
 for every such base point, not merely almost every base point.

Let c(s) be the maximum of χ on the circle |Q_base|²=exp s. It is finite and convex in s by the subharmonic three-circles theorem. A whole circle cannot be a polar exceptional set unless χ is identically -∞; that trivial competitor causes no issue. The bound c(s)≤max(0,s)+C forces every subgradient to lie in [0,1]. A negative subgradient would violate the bounded-above growth as s→-∞, and one exceeding 1 would violate it as s→+∞. Continuity of finite convex functions extends the obstacle bound c(s)≤s²/4 from (-2,4) to [-2,4]. Given any s and any p∈∂c(s), use the supporting-line inequality at 2p∈[0,2]:
 c(s)+p(2p-s)≤c(2p)≤p².
It follows that c(s)≤ps-p²≤g(s). Therefore χ(Q_base)≤g(log|Q_base|²), proving v≤P on the torus. Canonical psh representatives, or density followed by the submean property, extend this upper bound globally.

Conversely g is convex with slopes between 0 and 1, so χ_g(Q_base)=g(log|Q_base|²) is subharmonic and defines an ω_FS-psh potential on CP1 after subtracting log(1+|Q_base|²). It has the appropriate extensions at 0 and ∞. The associated global θ-psh P is given by the pencil construction of n1. Moreover
 -1≤g(s)-max(0,s)≤0,
 hence ψ-1≤P≤ψ and P belongs to the ordinary class and thus to the full ideal class. Finally,
 g(s)≤s²/4≤(x1²+x2²)/2=Q(x),
 so P≤w on all of K, pointwise. This proves that the supremum of all competitors is exactly P even before USC regularization. In particular the full ideal envelope is P. At the two poles its USC value remains -∞, since P has a logarithmic pole there.

2. Global lower bound from the actual ideal-selected Hilbert spaces.
All the following estimates concern the precise B_m and original Hilbert norm of the question. Use n2's exact orthogonal basis and norm formula. The diagonal sections s_jj, 0≤j≤m, are among the actual selected basis sections; their norm satisfies
 A_m(j,j)≤(2π/(9m))exp(j²/m).
Thus
 B_m≥(9m/(2π))exp(-mφ_X) max_{0≤j≤m}exp(js-j²/m).
For every real s,
 max_{0≤j≤m}[(j/m)s-(j/m)²]≥g(s)-1/(4m²).
Indeed when s≤0 or s≥2 the maximizing endpoint 0 or 1 belongs to the grid; when 0≤s≤2 choose the grid point nearest s/2 and the loss is its squared distance, at most 1/(4m²). Consequently
 U_m≥P+ (1/m)log(9m/(2π))-1/(4m²).                 (L)
This is a global envelope lower bound on the torus, and extends to X minus the poles by continuity. At the poles it has the natural inequality with right side -∞. Its error tends to zero independently of the point. In fact the displayed correction is positive for all m≥1, but only its vanishing is needed.

The use of diagonal sections for a lower bound does not replace the actual spaces: their full dimensions and the upper estimate below use all three bands. The full-envelope character of (L) rests on the non-toric competitor identification and envelope proof above, rather than on a toric-only spectrum computation.

3. Upper bound for the entire actual series and convergence topology.
The lower bound for A_m in n2 gives
 B_m≤C m exp(-mφ_X) Σ_{|a-b|≤1} exp(a x1+b x2-(a²+b²)/(2m)),
 with the sum also restricted to 0≤a,b≤m. For diagonal terms the exponent is at most m g(s). For a=j+1,b=j,
 exponent=js-j²/m+x1-(2j+1)/(2m)
 ≤m g(s)+x1.
Comparing instead with diagonal index j+1 gives
 exponent≤m g(s)-x2+1.
It is therefore bounded by m g(s)+log min(exp x1,exp(1-x2)). The other off-diagonal band is bounded in the same way with x1,x2 interchanged. Put
 R(x)=1+min(exp x1,exp(1-x2))+min(exp x2,exp(1-x1)).
Counting the diagonal and the two bands yields
 B_m≤C m(m+1)R(x)exp(mP(x)),
 hence
 U_m≤P+[C+2log(m+1)+log R(x)]/m.                 (U)
Changing C only enlarges the bound for finitely many m.

R has a continuous finite extension across the coordinate divisors away from p,q and is bounded on every compact subset of X\{p,q}. For example at z1=0 with z2 finite its value is 1+|z2|²; at z1=∞ with z2 finite it is 1+e/|z2|², with the simultaneous limiting cases at (0,0) and (∞,∞) equal to 1. Near p use A=|u|², B=|v|², with u=z1,v=1/z2. The potentially large term is min(1/B,e/A), and
 min(1/B,e/A)≤(e+1)/(A+B).
The other term stays bounded. The identical estimate holds near q. Thus, using any smooth distance,
 R≤C(1+dist(·,p)^(-2)+dist(·,q)^(-2)).
In particular log R is locally integrable and globally integrable against every smooth volume form on X.

It follows from (L) and (U) that:
 • U_m→P uniformly on every compact subset of X\{p,q}, with O(log m/m) error there. This includes coordinate-divisor points away from the poles, not only dense-torus compacta.
 • U_m→P globally in L¹ against a smooth volume form, with O(log m/m) error, by integrability of log R.
 • The convergence is global in the usual Kähler/Bedford–Taylor capacity: outside arbitrarily small neighborhoods of the two points it is uniform, and a finite pluripolar set has outer capacity zero.
 • The convergence holds pointwise as extended-real functions on all X. At each pole every section in V_m vanishes for m≥2, so U_m=-∞ there; P=-∞ there as well. For m=1 the space is the full four-dimensional H0(O(1,1)) and U_1 is finite at those points, which has no effect on convergence.

There is emphatically no global additive uniform error bound |U_m-P|. At either pole the least vanishing order in the entire V_m is m-1. Its leading local homogeneous forms include all degree-(m-1) binary monomials, so their sum of squares is comparable to r^{2(m-1)} in every direction, with constants allowed to depend on m. Consequently
 U_m=(1-1/m)log r²+O_m(1),
 P=log r²+O(1).
For every fixed m≥2, U_m-P tends to +∞ as r→0 on punctured approaches. This is precisely the failure of a uniform boundary/pole error estimate that would result from treating the actual multiplier ideals as order m rather than m-1.

One can also state a genuine global uniform topology without claiming an additive error: exp(U_m)→exp(P) uniformly on X. Indeed near a pole P≤log r²+C and R≤C/r². Estimate (U) yields
 U_m≤(1-1/m)log r²+C+[2log(m+1)+C]/m.
For m≥2 and r<1 this gives exp(U_m)≤C r with a constant independent of m. Also exp(P)≤C r². Uniform convergence away from the poles, together with these uniform smallness bounds near them, proves the assertion.

4. Final identifications and normalization.
The actual spaces are exactly n2's three-band spaces, with N_m=3m+1 and Hilbert growth exponent 1. The full ideal and ordinary θ-psh competitor classes coincide for arbitrary non-toric functions by n1; thus equality of their envelopes holds in particular for every smooth obstacle on all X. For this K and w the full envelope is the P displayed above, and the actual U_m satisfy the global envelope lower bound (L) and the convergence statements just proved. The normalized trace kernel measure is
 (3m+1)^(-1) B_m exp(-mw)ν,
 and n2 proves its weak limit is dt times independent normalized angular Haar on x1=x2=t∈[0,1]. The limit is supported on the contact set: g(2t)=t²=Q(t,t). With intrinsic m normalization rather than probability normalization the limit is three times this measure. Ambient m² normalization instead loses all mass. These results account for all global section constraints, the original Hilbert norms, and the actual rather than substituted ideal-selected spaces.

notes.summary: For arbitrary genuine, possibly non-toric θ-psh v, the full ideal class equals {v≤ψ+C}. At the two poles I(tψ)=m^{max(0,floor(t)-1)}. A precisely stated weighted point-extension input recovers the endpoint logarithmic bound; all local-integrability statements include connectedness and nontriviality. Every competitor factors through the pencil [T1T2:Z1Z2], and the two envelope constructions therefore agree for every smooth global obstacle.
notes.detailedSummary: This is a fresh argument, with no dependency on previous dead notes. Near either pole ψ=log max(|u|²,|v|²) minus a smooth metric potential, so radial integration gives the exact integer-sensitive ideals. Weighted Ohsawa–Takegoshi extension on connected balls implies that an ideal whose germs vanish to order k forces a genuine local psh potential φ to satisfy φ≤(k/t)log|z|²+C. Convexity of the radial maximum then gives the endpoint coefficient 1, despite the constants depending on t. This proves ideal/ordinary equality for every θ-psh function, not just toric ones. On generic smooth (1,1) pencil curves, the two unit pole atoms exhaust the curvature degree 2; hence the potential is constant along each such fiber after adding the torus metric potential. Fubini, restrictions to connected curves, and uniqueness of canonical psh representatives give the global description v=ψ_FS+u∘F for an arbitrary ω_FS-psh u on CP1. The only non-elementary existence theorem used is weighted L² hyperplane extension, with its exact exp(-Φ) statement and reduction to point extension specified for source verification. All its domains and restrictions here are connected and non-identically -∞.
notes.text:
This note reconstructs the class identification independently. No result from a dead note is used.

NORMALIZATIONS AND ANALYTIC INPUTS.
Set p=(0,∞), q=(∞,0), and write dd^c=(i/(2π))∂bar∂. Thus dd^c log|ζ|²=δ_0 in one variable, and ω_FS=dd^c log(1+|ζ|²) has integral 1 on CP1. A local metric potential φ_h means |e|_h²=e^{-φ_h}; consequently a local genuine psh potential of v is v+φ_h. Adding a smooth function does not change a multiplier ideal locally.

The standard elementary psh facts used have the following scope: on a CONNECTED complex manifold, a genuine psh function that is not identically -∞ is locally integrable; its canonical representative satisfies submean inequalities and is determined by its almost-everywhere values. Restrictions to connected complex submanifolds are psh or identically -∞; we only use their local integrability after establishing the former alternative. A psh function that is -∞ on a nonempty open subset of a connected domain is identically -∞. Thus, for a nontrivial global θ-psh v on connected X, no frame ball has identically -∞ potential. The identically -∞ global competitor is harmless and satisfies both constraints below.

Here is the precise non-elementary analytic input required. Weighted point extension on balls: if B_R⊂C^n is a Euclidean ball, 0<r<R, Φ is genuine psh on B_R, and a∈B_r with Φ(a)>-∞, then there is F∈O(B_R) with F(a)=1 and
 ∫_{B_R}|F|²e^{-Φ}dλ ≤ C_{n,R,r}e^{-Φ(a)}.                    (A)
The constant does not depend on Φ or a. This is a consequence of the weighted L² hyperplane extension theorem of T. Ohsawa and K. Takegoshi, “On the extension of L² holomorphic functions,” Math. Z. 195 (1987), 197–204. The exact primary-source formulation needed is: square-integrable holomorphic data on a complex hyperplane in a bounded pseudoconvex domain extend with their e^{-Φ} norm bounded by a constant independent of the psh weight, controlled by the domain's bounded normal coordinate. Only Euclidean balls and their affine slices are needed here. To derive (A), choose a flag of affine complex subspaces through a and extend successively from dimension zero to dimension n. Every slice is a connected ball, and every restricted weight is non-identically -∞ because it is finite at a. Their diameters are bounded by 2R, and a stays a uniformly positive distance from their boundaries when |a|≤r. The starting zero-dimensional norm is e^{-Φ(a)}. This proves the stated corollary with uniform constants.

This specifies the external theorem and the entire reduction actually used; no optimal extension constant is needed. All weights in this argument are exactly e^{-Φ}. If a source writes its weight as e^{-2φ}, its application here is φ=Φ/2. This relabeling leaves plurisubharmonicity unchanged. The curvature normalization dd^c does not enter (A), and there is no unexplained factor of two in the multiplier-ideal exponent. The primary-source dependency is the hyperplane extension theorem just stated, not a Bergman asymptotic, valuative ideal theorem, or envelope convergence theorem.

1. EXACT MULTIPLIER IDEALS OF ψ.
Near p use coordinates u=z1, v=1/z2 and frame T1 Z2. The two pencil sections T1T2 and Z1Z2 have coefficients v and u, respectively. The metric potential is
 φ_h=log(1+|u|²)+log(1+|v|²),
so
 ψ=log max(|u|²,|v|²)-φ_h.
The same formula holds at q after exchanging the two factors. Elsewhere ψ is locally bounded.

The maximum squared norm and |u|²+|v|² are comparable. If a nonzero holomorphic germ f has order k, its spherical squared mean is comparable, for small radius, to r^{2k}: the leading homogeneous polynomial has strictly positive spherical squared integral, and higher terms contribute lower-order errors. Integrability against e^{-tψ} is therefore equivalent to convergence of
 ∫_0^ε r^{2k-2t+3}dr,
which occurs exactly when k+2>t, with logarithmic divergence at equality. Hence
 I(tψ)_p=m_p^{k(t)},  I(tψ)_q=m_q^{k(t)},
 k(t)=max(0,floor(t)-1),                                      (1)
and I(tψ)=O away from p,q. In particular, I(mψ) has order m-1 at both poles for each integer m≥1.

2. RECOVERING THE LOGARITHMIC POLE FROM IDEAL CONTAINMENT.
We give the local argument, including its endpoint. Let φ be non-identically -∞ genuine psh on a connected ball centered at 0. Shrink the ball so that φ≤M on it; its closure lies in the original domain. Suppose every germ in I(tφ)_0 has order at least k. Every holomorphic f of finite weighted norm
 ||f||_t²=∫_B |f|²e^{-tφ}dλ
then has its jets of orders below k equal to zero. Since ||f||_{L²(B)}²≤e^{tM}||f||_t², the holomorphic L² Cauchy estimate and its Taylor remainder give, on a smaller fixed ball,
 |f(z)|²≤A_{t,k}|z|^{2k}||f||_t².                            (2)
For example this follows by expanding in Taylor monomials orthogonal on the ball: the terms of degrees <k vanish, and the remaining evaluation sum is bounded by a constant times |z|^{2k} on a smaller ball.

For φ(z)>-∞ apply (A) with Φ=tφ and a=z. Substitute the resulting f_z, with f_z(z)=1, into (2). This yields
 φ(z)≤(k/t)log|z|²+C_{t,k}.                                  (3)
At points with φ=-∞ it is automatic. If k>0, φ(0) cannot be finite: extension at 0 would contradict the forced vanishing. Thus the conclusion has the correct pointwise value at 0 also. No constant uniform in t or k is asserted or needed.

For the endpoint, put M_φ(s)=sup_{|z|≤e^{s/2}}φ(z), for sufficiently negative s. This is finite and nondecreasing. The one-variable three-circles theorem on each complex line through 0 shows it is convex: it is the supremum of the convex radial maxima on these lines. Restrictions that are identically -∞ do not affect that supremum. Let ν be its limiting left slope as s→-∞. It exists, is nonnegative and finite by convexity. If (3) holds with coefficient c, then M_φ(s)≤cs+C, which implies ν≥c. Also convexity gives
 M_φ(s)≤M_φ(s0)+ν(s-s0),  s<s0:                              (4)
the secant slope ending at s0 is at least the limiting left slope. In particular, if the coefficients in (3) approach 1, then ν≥1, and (4) implies φ(z)≤log|z|²+C. This is an endpoint bound; it does not take a limit of the uncontrolled constants in (3).

3. FULL IDEAL CLASS EQUALS THE ORDINARY BOUNDED-ABOVE TYPE CLASS.
Let v be any nontrivial genuine θ-psh function with I(tv)⊂I(tψ) for every real t>0. At either pole set φ=v+φ_h on its connected frame ball. The smooth metric potential leaves its multiplier ideals unchanged. Equations (1)–(3) apply with k=k(t), and k(t)/t→1 as t→∞. The endpoint argument gives
 v+φ_h≤log(|u|²+|v|²)+C.
Since log(|u|²+|v|²) differs from log max(|u|²,|v|²) by at most log 2, this is v≤ψ+C near each pole. On a compact complement of smaller pole neighborhoods, ψ is continuous and finite and v is bounded above. Combining these bounds gives one finite global C_v with v≤ψ+C_v.

Conversely, v≤ψ+C_v implies
 e^{-tψ}≤e^{tC_v}e^{-tv}.
Every germ integrable against the latter is integrable against the former. Consequently, for ALL genuine θ-psh functions, with no invariance assumption,
 {v:v≤_Iψ}={v:v≤ψ+C_v for some finite C_v}.                    (5)
Both sets contain the identically -∞ function if it is allowed. Equality holds before imposing any obstacle, so all their obstacle-restricted suprema and USC regularizations agree. In particular their envelopes agree for every smooth obstacle on all X, as well as for the compact-obstacle problem in the question.

4. COMPLETE NON-TORIC PENCIL DESCRIPTION.
Off p,q define
 F=[T1T2:Z1Z2],
 ψ_FS=log(|T1T2|_h²+|Z1Z2|_h²).
Then ψ≤ψ_FS≤ψ+log 2. On the torus, with Q=z1z2, s=log|Q|² and φ_X=log(1+e^{x1})+log(1+e^{x2}),
 ψ_FS=log(1+|Q|²)-φ_X.

For Q∈C*, the closed curve C_Q={Z1Z2=Q T1T2} is a connected smooth rational (1,1) curve, parameterized by z1 with z2=Q/z1. It passes through p and q. Since each projection has degree 1, ∫_{C_Q}θ=2. If v|C_Q is not identically -∞, it is a genuine θ|C_Q-psh function on a connected compact curve, hence locally integrable. The bound v≤ψ+C implies in a local parameter at either pole a bound log|ζ|²+O(1) for its local psh potential. The atom of the one-variable curvature measure is therefore at least 1 at each pole, by the elementary Jensen/Lelong slope formula. The curvature measure θ|C_Q+dd^c(v|C_Q) has total mass 2 by Stokes. It must be exactly δ_p+δ_q.

On the same curve, T1T2 has precisely two simple zeros, p and q, and the ratio Z1Z2/(T1T2) is constant. Thus θ|C_Q+dd^c(ψ|C_Q)=δ_p+δ_q also. It follows that v|C_Q-ψ|C_Q is distributionally harmonic and therefore a constant on the compact connected curve. Canonical representatives make this equality pointwise. Equivalently, v+φ_X is constant along its torus fiber.

The local integrability of v on the torus and Fubini in holomorphic coordinates (z1,Q) show that almost every fiber has non-identically -∞ restriction. Let S={z1=1}, identified with CP1 by Q=z2. Each of those good fibers has a finite value at its point on S, by the just-proved constancy. Therefore v|S is a nontrivial genuine ω_FS-psh function on connected S. Define u=v|S+log 2. Here θ|S=ω_FS and ψ_FS|S=-log 2, so the constants are fixed by the actual product metric.

The fiber calculation gives, almost everywhere on the torus,
 v=ψ_FS+u∘F.                                                (6)
The right side has genuine psh local potentials off p,q: its curvature is F*(ω_FS+dd^c u). Both sides have canonical representatives, hence (6) holds everywhere off p,q. At either base point, u is bounded above on compact CP1 and ψ_FS has a logarithmic pole; their psh removable extension has value -∞. The bound already proved for v gives the same value there. Thus (6) holds globally with these extensions.

Conversely, any nontrivial ω_FS-psh u on CP1 gives this construction. In a frame with pencil coefficients a,b, its local potential off the common zeros is
 log(|a|²+|b|²)+u([a:b]),
which is psh and bounded above by log(|a|²+|b|²)+C. The standard removable-extension principle for a locally bounded-above psh function across an isolated analytic set gives its canonical extension at the common zeros, with value -∞ by this bound. reconstruction.statement:
Let X=CP¹×CP¹, L=O(1,1), and h be the product Fubini–Study metric. Use dd^c=(i/(2π))∂∂̄, θ=c₁(L,h), and local metric potentials defined by |e|²_h=e^(−φ_h). Thus dd^c log|ζ|²=δ₀ and ∫_{CP¹}ω_FS=1. Every θ-psh function below has genuine plurisubharmonic local potentials v+φ_h with their canonical upper representatives. Put p=(0,∞), q=(∞,0), and ψ=max(log|T₁T₂|²_h,log|Z₁Z₂|²_h). The multiplier ideal I(tv) consists of germs f for which |f|²e^(−tv) is locally integrable, and v≤_Iψ means I(tv)⊆I(tψ) for every real t>0.

1. In coordinates (u,η)=(z₁,1/z₂) at p, with frame T₁Z₂, and in coordinates (u,η)=(1/z₁,z₂) at q, with frame Z₁T₂, one has φ_h=log(1+|u|²)+log(1+|η|²) and ψ=log max(|u|²,|η|²)−φ_h. Elsewhere ψ is locally bounded. For every real t>0,
I(tψ)_p=m_p^{k(t)},  I(tψ)_q=m_q^{k(t)},  k(t)=max(0,⌊t⌋−1),
and I(tψ)=O_X away from p,q. Equivalently, a nonzero germ of order k at either pole belongs to I(tψ) exactly when k+2>t. In particular, I(mψ) has order m−1 at both poles for every integer m≥1.

2. For every integer n≥1 and 0<r<R, there is a constant C_{n,R,r}, independent of the weight and point, with the following property. If Φ is genuine psh on the Euclidean ball B_R⊂Cⁿ and a∈B_r satisfies Φ(a)>−∞, there exists F∈O(B_R) such that F(a)=1 and
∫_{B_R}|F|²e^(−Φ)dλ≤C_{n,R,r}e^(−Φ(a)).
The exponent here is exactly −Φ.

3. Let φ be non-identically −∞ and genuine psh on a connected ball centered at 0 in Cⁿ. For t>0 and an integer k≥0, the hypothesis I(tφ)_0⊆m₀^k implies, on a smaller neighborhood of 0,
φ(z)≤(k/t)log|z|²+C_{t,k},
for a finite constant; when k>0 it also implies φ(0)=−∞. No uniformity in t or k is asserted. More precisely, choose a smaller ball B on which φ≤M. Under the same ideal-containment hypothesis, every f∈O(B) of finite norm ||f||²_t=∫_B|f|²e^(−tφ)dλ has all jets of orders below k equal to zero, and on a fixed smaller ball satisfies
|f(z)|²≤A_{t,k}|z|^{2k}||f||²_t,
with A_{t,k} independent of f and z.

For sufficiently negative s, define M_φ(s)=sup_{|z|≤e^(s/2)}φ(z). This is finite, nondecreasing, and convex. Its limiting left slope ν as s→−∞ exists and is finite and nonnegative. If φ(z)≤c log|z|²+C near 0, then ν≥c. For s<s₀ in the domain of M_φ,
M_φ(s)≤M_φ(s₀)+ν(s−s₀).
In particular, logarithmic upper bounds with coefficients tending to 1 imply the endpoint bound φ(z)≤log|z|²+C near 0. Hence I(tφ)_0⊆m₀^{max(0,⌊t⌋−1)} for every real t>0 implies that endpoint bound.

4. For every genuine θ-psh function v on X, without any toric or angular-invariance assumption,
v≤_Iψ ⇔ there exists a finite constant C_v such that v≤ψ+C_v on X.
If the identically −∞ function is allowed, it belongs to both classes. For every nontrivial v satisfying the ideal constraint, the local potential at each pole satisfies v+φ_h≤log(|u|²+|η|²)+C; in particular v(p)=v(q)=−∞.

5. Define F=[T₁T₂:Z₁Z₂] on X\{p,q} and ψ_FS=log(|T₁T₂|²_h+|Z₁Z₂|²_h). Then ψ≤ψ_FS≤ψ+log 2. Every nontrivial member of the class in part 4 has a unique representation
v=ψ_FS+u∘F on X\{p,q},
where u is a non-identically −∞ genuine ω_FS-psh function on CP¹. The function v has the canonical θ-psh extension with value −∞ at both base points. Conversely, every such u defines a genuine θ-psh function in the class by this formula and canonical extension. Off the base points its curvature is F*(ω_FS+dd^c u). In a local frame with pencil coefficients a,b, its local psh potential is log(|a|²+|b|²)+u([a:b]).

For S={z₁=1}≅CP¹, one has θ|_S=ω_FS, ψ_FS|_S=−log 2, and u=v|_S+log 2; this restriction is nontrivial. On the dense torus, write Q=z₁z₂, x_i=log|z_i|², and φ_X=log(1+e^{x₁})+log(1+e^{x₂}). The representation is equivalently
v=χ(Q)−φ_X,
where χ(Q)=log(1+|Q|²)+u(Q) is subharmonic on C and satisfies χ(Q)≤max(0,log|Q|²)+C on C*.

For each Q∈C*, the curve C_Q={Z₁Z₂=Q T₁T₂} is a connected smooth rational (1,1) curve containing p and q, and ∫_{C_Q}θ=2. For a class member v whose restriction to C_Q is not identically −∞,
θ|_{C_Q}+dd^c(v|_{C_Q})=δ_p+δ_q=θ|_{C_Q}+dd^c(ψ|_{C_Q}),
and v|_{C_Q}=ψ|_{C_Q}+c_Q for a finite constant c_Q, with the equality interpreted in extended values at the poles. Almost every Q∈C*, with respect to planar Lebesgue measure, has a non-identically −∞ restriction.

6. For every compact K⊂X and continuous real obstacle w on K, the USC regularized supremum over genuine θ-psh functions satisfying v≤_Iψ and v≤w quasi-everywhere on K equals the USC regularized supremum with the ideal constraint replaced by v≤ψ+C_v for some finite C_v. The unregularized suprema also agree. In particular, the two envelope constructions agree for every smooth real obstacle on all of X.
reconstruction.proof:
We use exactly the three supplied external premises. In particular, the extension weight is exp(−Φ), not exp(−2Φ). All functions and restrictions used below have their genuine psh or subharmonic representatives.

1. Local ideals and normalization. In the frame T₁Z₂ at p, the two pencil sections have coefficients η and u. In the frame Z₁T₂ at q, they have coefficients u and η. Both frames have metric potential log(1+|u|²)+log(1+|η|²). Consequently the asserted expressions for ψ hold. The pencil coefficients have no common zero elsewhere, so ψ is locally bounded off p,q. Its local potentials are maxima of logarithms of squared absolute values of holomorphic functions, hence are genuinely psh.

Write r²=|u|²+|η|². Since r²/2≤max(|u|²,|η|²)≤r², the density exp(−tψ) is comparable, on a sufficiently small coordinate ball, to r^(−2t). If a nonzero holomorphic germ f has order k and leading homogeneous term f_k, then
∫_{|ξ|=1}|f(rξ)|²dσ(ξ)=r^(2k)(∫|f_k|²dσ+O(r)),
where the leading integral is positive. Thus its weighted integral converges exactly when ∫₀^ε r^(2k−2t+3)dr converges, namely when k+2>t. This proves I(tψ)=m^{max(0,⌊t⌋−1)} at each pole, including the integer thresholds. Away from them the ideal is the full structure sheaf. The coefficient one in these logarithms agrees with dd^c log|ζ|²=δ₀; each factor's Fubini–Study form has mass one.

2. Point extension from the stated hyperplane premise. Choose an affine orthogonal flag E₀={a}⊂E₁⊂⋯⊂E_n=Cⁿ through a. Each B_R∩E_j is a Euclidean ball of radius at most R, and B_R∩E_{j−1} is its intersection with an affine complex hyperplane. Every restricted weight is genuine psh and not identically −∞, since its value at a is finite. Start with the function 1 on E₀, whose weighted integral is exp(−Φ(a)). Apply the supplied premise successively in dimensions 1,…,n. At every step the preceding integral is finite, the extension preserves the value at a, and the constant is independent of the position of the hyperplane and the weight. The resulting F satisfies
F(a)=1,  ∫_{B_R}|F|²exp(−Φ)≤(∏_{j=1}^n C(j,R))exp(−Φ(a)).
This gives the claimed C_{n,R,r} (in fact this construction needs no additional dependence on r). All intersections and measures here are the Euclidean ones required by the premise.

3. Ideal containment forces logarithmic upper bounds. Choose a ball B compactly contained in the original ball, centered at zero, on which φ≤M. A holomorphic f of finite weighted norm on B belongs, as a germ, to I(tφ)_0. Hence the containment hypothesis kills all its Taylor coefficients of degree less than k. Furthermore
∫_B|f|²≤exp(tM)||f||²_t.
The unweighted holomorphic submean inequality and Cauchy estimates on nested smaller balls bound all Taylor coefficients in terms of exp(tM/2)||f||_t. Summing the Taylor series after its first k vanishing degrees gives, on a fixed sufficiently small ball,
|f(z)|²≤A_{t,k}|z|^(2k)||f||²_t.
The constant may depend on the weight, the balls, t and k, but not on f or z, as asserted.

For a point z in this smaller ball with φ(z)>−∞, apply part 2 on B to the genuine psh weight tφ. The resulting function F_z has F_z(z)=1 and ||F_z||²_t≤C exp(−tφ(z)). The jet estimate therefore gives
1≤A_{t,k}C|z|^(2k)exp(−tφ(z)),
which rearranges to φ(z)≤(k/t)log|z|²+C_{t,k}. At points where φ=−∞ the bound is automatic. If k>0 and φ(0) were finite, point extension at zero would produce a finite-norm function with value one, contradicting the killed constant jet. Thus φ(0)=−∞ in that case.

Here is the endpoint argument, including why varying constants cause no difficulty. For sufficiently negative s, M_φ(s)=sup_{|z|≤exp(s/2)}φ(z) is finite and nondecreasing. It is convex: restrict φ to each complex line through zero and apply the annular subharmonic maximum principle against the harmonic function affine in log|ζ|² joining the bounds at two radii; then take the supremum over directions. The maximum on a ball equals the maximum on its boundary by the same linewise maximum principle. Finite convexity implies that the limiting left slope ν exists. Nondecreasingness gives ν≥0, and any slope at a fixed interior s bounds it above, so ν is finite. Integrating the slope inequality yields
M_φ(s)≤M_φ(s₀)+ν(s−s₀),  s<s₀.
Also lim_{s→−∞}M_φ(s)/s=ν: this follows directly by bounding the slopes between ν and ν+ε sufficiently far to the left and integrating. Thus M_φ(s)≤cs+C for all sufficiently negative s implies ν≥c. If logarithmic bounds have coefficients tending to one, their neighborhoods and constants may vary, but each separately implies its corresponding lower bound on this same ν. Hence ν≥1. Since s−s₀<0, the displayed inequality gives M_φ(s)≤s+C, and therefore φ(z)≤log|z|²+C. Applying this with k(t)=max(0,⌊t⌋−1), for which k(t)/t→1, proves the final assertion of part 3.

4. Equality of the two complete competitor classes. Suppose v is nontrivial and satisfies the ideal constraint. Near either pole put φ=v+φ_h. Addition of the smooth φ_h leaves every local multiplier ideal unchanged, since its exponential is bounded above and below on a smaller ball. This φ is genuine psh and not identically −∞. Parts 1 and 3 therefore imply
v+φ_h≤log(|u|²+|η|²)+C.
Comparison with log max(|u|²,|η|²) proves v≤ψ+C near each pole, and also v(p)=v(q)=−∞. On the complement of small pole neighborhoods, ψ is bounded below and v is bounded above, so a finite global C_v follows.

Conversely, v≤ψ+C_v implies exp(−tψ)≤exp(tC_v)exp(−tv). Integrability of |f|²exp(−tv) thus implies integrability of |f|²exp(−tψ), at every point and for every real t>0. This proves the reverse implication. The identically −∞ function belongs to both classes, with zero multiplier ideals. None of this argument assumes angular invariance.

5. Descent through the pencil. First consider C_Q for Q∈C*. It is the graph of the automorphism z↦Q/z of CP¹, hence is a connected smooth rational (1,1) curve. It contains p,q, and both projections have degree one, so ∫_{C_Q}θ=2. Near p its coordinates satisfy η=u/Q, and near q they satisfy the analogous nonzero linear relation. Thus ψ restricted to this curve has a logarithmic pole of coefficient one at each point. More explicitly, T₁T₂ restricted to C_Q is a section with precisely these two simple zeros, and ψ|_{C_Q}=log|T₁T₂|²_h+max(0,log|Q|²) away from them. Therefore θ|_{C_Q}+dd^c(ψ|_{C_Q})=δ_p+δ_q.

If v|_{C_Q} is nontrivial, it is genuinely θ|_{C_Q}-psh. The ordinary upper bound from part 4 gives a coefficient-one logarithmic upper bound at both poles for its local subharmonic potentials. The supplied atom premise, with c=1 and precisely the prescribed dd^c normalization, implies that its positive curvature measure has an atom of mass at least one at each pole. Its total mass is exactly two by Stokes. Hence the entire measure is δ_p+δ_q. The difference of the two restricted potentials is harmonic as a distribution on CP¹ and therefore is a constant. Their genuine representatives give v|_{C_Q}=ψ|_{C_Q}+c_Q, including the extended values at the poles.

Almost every restriction is nontrivial. Indeed, on the torus use holomorphic coordinates (z₁,Q=z₁z₂). A nontrivial genuine local psh potential is locally integrable. Fubini on relatively compact product charts implies that for almost every Q it is finite at almost every z₁ in a fixed annulus, which rules out an identically −∞ restriction. A countable collection of Q-annuli proves the assertion on C*.

This also proves descent without assuming toricity and without permitting exceptional upward values. Set f(z₁,Q)=v(z₁,Q/z₁)+φ_X(z₁,Q/z₁) on C*×C*. It is genuine psh. For every Q with nontrivial restriction the preceding constant formula says that f(z₁,Q) is independent of z₁. In particular f(1,Q) is finite for almost every Q. Thus its restriction to z₁=1 is a nontrivial genuine subharmonic function χ(Q). For almost every Q, f(z₁,Q)=χ(Q) for every z₁. Consequently f and the genuine psh function χ(Q) agree almost everywhere on the torus and hence agree everywhere. The last implication uses canonical representatives: a genuine psh value is the limit of its ball averages, by submean and upper semicontinuity, so almost-everywhere equality determines every value, also at −∞ points.

The section S={z₁=1} is a copy of CP¹ with θ|_S=ω_FS. Its restriction is nontrivial by the preceding almost-everywhere statement. Direct evaluation gives ψ_FS|_S=−log 2. Hence
u=v|_S+log 2
is a nontrivial genuine ω_FS-psh function on CP¹, and χ(Q)=log(1+|Q|²)+u(Q). Thus on the torus v=ψ_FS+u∘F=χ(Q)−φ_X.

For completeness this formula is genuine psh on all of X outside the two base points, not just on the torus. In a frame let a,b be the pencil coefficients. Where a≠0 its local potential equals
log|a|²+[log(1+|b/a|²)+u([1:b/a])],
a pluriharmonic function plus a holomorphic pullback of a genuine subharmonic potential. The analogous expression applies where b≠0. The formula agrees with v on the torus, so canonical uniqueness extends equality to every non-base point. Its curvature there is F*(ω_FS+dd^c u), with this pullback defined by precisely these local potentials. Restriction to S proves uniqueness of u. The ordinary bound on the torus gives χ(Q)≤max(0,log|Q|²)+C.

Conversely, let u be any nontrivial genuine ω_FS-psh function on CP¹. It is bounded above on that compact space. The same local expression is genuine psh off the base points and is not identically −∞. Near a base point it is bounded above by log(|a|²+|b|²)+sup u, which tends to −∞. The supplied analytic-extension premise therefore gives its canonical psh extension with value −∞ at both base points. It defines a global θ-psh v. Since ψ≤ψ_FS≤ψ+log 2, it satisfies v≤ψ+C and hence the ideal constraint by part 4. This proves all representation assertions.

6. Since part 4 identifies the whole classes pointwise, intersecting either class with the identical quasi-everywhere obstacle condition gives identical sets of competitors for every compact K and continuous w. Their unregularized suprema are equal, and so are their USC regularizations. In particular this holds for every smooth obstacle on all X. No unlisted envelope or Bergman convergence theorem has been used.
