This note uses only n1's exact local multiplier-ideal computation.

1. ENTIRE ACTUAL SPACES AND GROWTH.
For m≥1 a basis of H0(X,O(m,m)) is
 s_ab=Z1^a T1^{m-a} Z2^b T2^{m-b},  0≤a,b≤m.
At p, in the frame T1^m Z2^m, this is u^a v^{m-b}; at q it has order b+m-a. By n1 the required ideal orders are m-1 at both points. The conditions are exactly
 a+m-b≥m-1,  b+m-a≥m-1,
i.e. |a-b|≤1. For a general section, the local monomial exponents are distinct; terms of insufficient degree cannot cancel as polynomials. Therefore
 V_m=span{s_ab:0≤a,b≤m, |a-b|≤1}.                            (7)
There are m+1 diagonal elements and m elements on each adjacent diagonal, hence
 N_m=dim V_m=3m+1,  m≥1.                                   (8)
With the natural V_0=C this formula also gives N_0=1. The intrinsic Hilbert growth exponent lim(log N_m)/(log m) is 1, and N_m/m→3. Equivalently the leading dimension coefficient with this growth normalization is 3.

The selection at the single exponent m must not be confused with sections whose own potential (1/m)log|s|_{h^m}² belongs to n1's ordinary class. Those must have order at least m at both poles and are exactly the diagonal span, of dimension m+1. Equation (5) of n1 does not change this fact about the single-exponent section spaces. In particular the V_m are not a multiplicative graded ring: the square of Z1T2∈V_1 has offset 2 and is not in V_2. Ratios of suitable elements of V_m recover both z1 and z2 on the torus, so their rational-map images can have dimension 2. That does not change the growth exponent 1; graded-ring Iitaka assertions do not apply to this nonmultiplicative family.

2. EXACT ORIGINAL NORMS AND THE KERNEL.
Let
 φ_X(x)=log(1+e^{x1})+log(1+e^{x2}),
 H(x)=(x1²+x2²)/2,
 w=H-φ_X.
For s_ab one has
 |s_ab|_{h^m}²=exp(a x1+b x2-mφ_X).
Independent normalized angular Haar makes all distinct monomials orthogonal. Since the metric part of w cancels exactly, the ORIGINAL squared norm is
 A_m(a,b)=||s_ab||²=(1/9)I_m(a/m)I_m(b/m),                   (9)
 I_m(p)=∫_{-1}^2 exp(m(px-x²/2))dx
       =exp(mp²/2)J_m(p),
 J_m(p)=∫_{-1}^2 exp(-m(x-p)²/2)dx.
Thus s_ab/√A_m(a,b) over the complete set (7) is an orthonormal basis and
 B_m=exp(-mφ_X)∑_{(a,b) in (7)} exp(a x1+b x2)/A_m(a,b).     (10)
All angles disappear from the kernel.

For p∈[0,1] the center is at distance at least 1 from both endpoints of [-1,2]. Each omitted Gaussian tail is at most e^{-m/2}/m. Consequently, uniformly in all relevant p,
 J_m(p)=√(2π/m)(1+O(m^{-1/2}e^{-m/2})).                    (11)
The following nonasymptotic bounds, valid for every m≥1, are useful:
 c/√m≤J_m(p)≤√(2π/m),  c=∫_{-1}^1e^{-y²/2}dy.
For the lower bound integrate over [p-1/√m,p+1/√m], which is contained in [-1,2]. In particular
 (c²/(9m))exp((a²+b²)/(2m))≤A_m(a,b)
 ≤(2π/(9m))exp((a²+b²)/(2m)).                              (12)
No substituted Hilbert structure has been used.

3. NORMALIZED KERNEL-MEASURE LIMIT.
The probability trace measure associated with this Hilbert norm is
 μ_m=N_m^{-1}B_m e^{-mw}ν.                                  (13)
The weight e^{-mw} is essential; its total mass is exactly 1 by the orthonormal basis identity. Substitution of (9)–(10), including the original factor 1/9 in ν, shows that the contribution of each basis vector is precisely
 [e^{-m(x1-a/m)²/2}/J_m(a/m)]
 [e^{-m(x2-b/m)²/2}/J_m(b/m)] dx1 dx2
 ×dθ1/(2π)dθ2/(2π),
restricted to [-1,2]^2. Thus μ_m is the arithmetic average of these N_m product truncated-Gaussian probability measures.

Their masses outside any fixed positive-radius neighborhood of their centers tend to zero uniformly in the selected indices, by Gaussian tail bounds and the lower bound for J_m. For a continuous test function on K, uniform continuity reduces the integral to the average of its angularly averaged values at the centers, with an error tending to zero. The three bands have centers
 (j/m,j/m), 0≤j≤m;
 ((j+1)/m,j/m), 0≤j≤m-1;
 (j/m,(j+1)/m), 0≤j≤m-1.
Their three Riemann sums have the same limiting integral over t∈[0,1], and their relative cardinalities tend to 1/3 each. Therefore, weakly on X,
 μ_m→μ,
 ∫f dμ=∫_0^1∫_0^{2π}∫_0^{2π}
 f(e^{t/2+iθ1},e^{t/2+iθ2}) dθ1/(2π)dθ2/(2π)dt.             (14)
This is the probability measure dt times independent normalized angular Haar on x1=x2=t, 0≤t≤1. The measures normalized instead by the intrinsic power m satisfy
 m^{-1}B_m e^{-mw}ν→3μ.
Normalization by the ambient power m² yields zero. These statements account for both the intrinsic leading coefficient and the probability normalization.

The distinction between this nonmultiplicative family, its growth exponent 1, and the two-dimensional images of its rational maps is correct.

The original metric and obstacle cancel in the norm exactly as stated. Angular orthogonality, the factor 1/9, completion of squares, both Gaussian bounds, and the uniform tail estimate all check. In particular, the weighted trace measure is exactly an average of product truncated-Gaussian probabilities, not an approximation based on a substituted norm. Uniform concentration and the three lattice-band Riemann sums give the stated diagonal/Haar probability limit. Normalization by m gives three times that limit, whereas normalization by m² gives zero.

Both summaries accurately preserve the full-space identification, normalization, and nonmultiplicativity qualifications. No additional nonroutine external premise is needed beyond the declared established support.

reconstruction.report: Using n1, both pole constraints give exactly |a−b|≤1; distinct Taylor monomials cannot cancel prohibited orders. The dimension, nonmultiplicativity, and distinction from ordinary-type section potentials are correct. The original Hilbert norm yields the stated Gaussian factors and uniform estimates, including their constants. reconstruction.statement:
Let X=CP¹×CP¹, L=O(1,1) with the product Fubini–Study metric h, and ψ=max(log|T₁T₂|²_h,log|Z₁Z₂|²_h), with multiplier ideals defined by integrability of |f|²e^(−tψ). For integers m≥1 let V_m=H⁰(X,L^m⊗I(mψ)). In the dense torus use z_i=Z_i/T_i and x_i=log|z_i|². Put D=[−1,2]², let K consist of all points with x∈D and all angles, and set
φ_X(x)=log(1+e^{x₁})+log(1+e^{x₂}),  H(x)=(x₁²+x₂²)/2,  w=H−φ_X,
ν=(1/9)dx₁dx₂·dθ₁/(2π)·dθ₂/(2π).
Use the original squared Hilbert norm ||s||²_m=∫_K|s|²_{h^m}e^(−mw)dν. Let B_m be the sum of squared h^m norms of an orthonormal basis and U_m=m^(−1)log B_m.

1. Define s_ab=Z₁^aT₁^{m−a}Z₂^bT₂^{m−b}. The entire selected space is
V_m=span{s_ab:0≤a,b≤m, |a−b|≤1},
and these monomials form a basis. Thus N_m=dim V_m=3m+1 for every m≥1. With V₀=C, N₀=1 as well. The intrinsic Hilbert growth exponent is
lim_{m→∞}(log N_m)/(log m)=1,
and N_m/m→3.

For a nonzero global section s∈H⁰(X,L^m), the potential m^(−1)log|s|²_{h^m} is bounded above by ψ plus a finite constant exactly when s vanishes to order at least m at both p=(0,∞) and q=(∞,0). Those sections are exactly the diagonal subspace span{s_jj:0≤j≤m}, of dimension m+1, not the whole V_m. The family (V_m) is not multiplicative: Z₁T₂∈V₁ but (Z₁T₂)²∉V₂. On the dense torus, ratios of suitable elements of V_m recover both z₁ and z₂; the associated rational maps have two-dimensional image, despite the growth exponent being 1.

2. All distinct s_ab are orthogonal for the original Hilbert norm. For 0≤a,b≤m,
|s_ab|²_{h^m}=exp(a x₁+b x₂−mφ_X),
A_m(a,b):=||s_ab||²_m=(1/9)I_m(a/m)I_m(b/m),
where
I_m(p)=∫_{−1}²exp(m(px−x²/2))dx=exp(mp²/2)J_m(p),
J_m(p)=∫_{−1}²exp(−m(x−p)²/2)dx.
Consequently {s_ab/√A_m(a,b):0≤a,b≤m, |a−b|≤1} is an orthonormal basis of the entire V_m, and on the dense torus
B_m(x)=e^(−mφ_X(x))∑_{0≤a,b≤m, |a−b|≤1}exp(a x₁+b x₂)/A_m(a,b).
In particular, B_m is independent of the angles.

Uniformly for p∈[0,1], as m→∞,
J_m(p)=√(2π/m)(1+O(m^(−1/2)e^(−m/2))).
For every integer m≥1 and p∈[0,1], with c=∫_{−1}¹e^(−y²/2)dy,
c/√m≤J_m(p)≤√(2π/m).
Hence for every 0≤a,b≤m,
(c²/(9m))exp((a²+b²)/(2m))≤A_m(a,b)≤(2π/(9m))exp((a²+b²)/(2m)).

3. The weighted kernel trace measure
μ_m=(3m+1)^(−1)B_m e^(−mw)ν,
viewed as a measure on X supported on K, is a probability measure. It is exactly the arithmetic average, over all indices 0≤a,b≤m with |a−b|≤1, of the probability measures on K with densities
[e^(−m(x₁−a/m)²/2)/J_m(a/m)]·[e^(−m(x₂−b/m)²/2)/J_m(b/m)]dx₁dx₂·dθ₁/(2π)·dθ₂/(2π).

These measures satisfy μ_m⇀μ weakly on X, where for every continuous f on X,
∫_X f dμ=∫₀¹∫₀^{2π}∫₀^{2π}f(z₁=e^{t/2+iθ₁},z₂=e^{t/2+iθ₂}) dθ₁/(2π)dθ₂/(2π)dt.
Thus μ is dt on x₁=x₂=t, 0≤t≤1, times independent normalized angular Haar. With intrinsic power normalization,
m^(−1)B_m e^(−mw)ν⇀3μ,
whereas m^(−2)B_m e^(−mw)ν⇀0.
reconstruction.proof:
We use the proved claims of n1, in particular its exact integer multiplier ideals and normalization.

1. The complete spaces. Every section of O(m,m) is a unique linear combination of the s_ab with 0≤a,b≤m. In the frame (T₁Z₂)^m at p its coefficient is u^aη^(m−b), of order a+m−b. In the frame (Z₁T₂)^m at q its coefficient is u^(m−a)η^b, of order m−a+b. The ideal I(mψ) requires order at least m−1 at each point. These two conditions are exactly a−b≥−1 and a−b≤1.

This argument applies to arbitrary linear combinations: in either frame distinct pairs (a,b) give distinct monomials, so cancellation cannot remove an individual forbidden Taylor coefficient. There are no further conditions away from the two poles. Thus the displayed band of monomials is the entire selected space. It has m+1 diagonal elements and m elements on each adjacent diagonal, giving N_m=3m+1. With V₀=C one has N₀=1. Consequently log N_m/log m→1 and N_m/m→3.

For any nonzero section s, the ordinary type bound near a pole is equivalent to |f(u,η)|≤C(|u|²+|η|²)^(m/2) for its local coefficient f. Taylor expansion shows this is equivalent to vanishing order at least m; conversely that order gives the bound on a smaller ball. Off the poles the global ordinary bound follows from compactness. Repeating the two monomial-order tests with threshold m gives a−b≥0 and a−b≤0, so precisely the diagonal subspace is of ordinary type, and its dimension is m+1. This does not identify it with V_m: the ideals use threshold m−1.

At m=1 there is no imposed vanishing, so Z₁T₂∈V₁. Its square has nonzero value at q in its local frame and therefore is not in V₂, which requires order one there. Hence these spaces do not form a multiplicative series. For every m≥1, s₀₀,s₁₀,s₀₁ all belong to V_m, and on the torus s₁₀/s₀₀=z₁, s₀₁/s₀₀=z₂. The corresponding rational map therefore has two-dimensional image. This is compatible with growth exponent one because multiplicativity is absent.

2. Original norms and kernels. The squared metric norm is
|s_ab|²_{h^m}=exp(a x₁+b x₂−mφ_X).
Multiplication by exp(−mw)=exp(−mH+mφ_X) cancels the metric factor exactly. Distinct monomials are orthogonal because their angular characters are distinct and the measure uses independent normalized Haar. For every pair 0≤a,b≤m, whether selected or not,
A_m(a,b)=(1/9)∫_{−1}²exp(a x₁−mx₁²/2)dx₁ ∫_{−1}²exp(b x₂−mx₂²/2)dx₂
=(1/9)I_m(a/m)I_m(b/m).
Completing the square gives I_m(p)=exp(mp²/2)J_m(p) with the claimed J_m. Consequently the normalized selected monomials form an orthonormal basis of the entire space and yield exactly the stated angularly invariant kernel formula.

Here are uniform estimates, including the endpoints p=0,1. Under y=√m(x−p), the interval contains [−√m,√m]. The omitted Gaussian tails are bounded by
2∫_{√m}^∞exp(−y²/2)dy≤2m^(−1/2)exp(−m/2).
Therefore
J_m(p)=√(2π/m)(1+O(m^(−1/2)exp(−m/2)))
uniformly for p∈[0,1]. For all m≥1, the interval [p−1/√m,p+1/√m] lies in [−1,2]. Integration over that interval gives c/√m≤J_m(p), where c=∫_{−1}¹exp(−y²/2)dy. Integration over the whole real line gives the upper bound √(2π/m). Applying these two bounds to both factors proves all asserted estimates for A_m, with exactly the original factor 1/9.

3. Kernel-measure limit. Orthogonality and normalization give
∫_K B_m exp(−mw)dν=N_m.
Thus μ_m is a probability measure. The contribution of the normalized monomial (a,b) to the unnormalized trace measure is
exp(a x₁+b x₂−mH)/(I_m(a/m)I_m(b/m)) dx₁dx₂·dθ₁/(2π)·dθ₂/(2π).
Completing the squares cancels the constants exp((a²+b²)/(2m)) and gives exactly the product of truncated Gaussian probability densities in the statement. In particular the factor 1/9 has canceled, rather than changing the limiting normalization.

These Gaussian measures concentrate uniformly at their centers. Indeed, for every p∈[0,1],
(1/J_m(p))∫_{−1}²(x−p)²exp(−m(x−p)²/2)dx≤C/m,
using the lower bound c/√m and the full-line second Gaussian moment. Chebyshev's inequality and uniform continuity on the compact K show that for every continuous f on X the integral of f against a monomial probability measure differs, uniformly in the selected pair, by o(1) from
T_f(a/m,b/m),
where T_f(p,q) is the normalized angular average of f at z₁=exp(p/2+iθ₁), z₂=exp(q/2+iθ₂). This T_f is continuous on [0,1]². Since |a−b|≤1, uniform continuity further replaces T_f(a/m,b/m) by T_f(a/m,a/m), with a uniform o(1) error.

The three index families now give the three Riemann sums
∑_{j=0}^m T_f(j/m,j/m),
∑_{j=1}^m T_f(j/m,j/m),
∑_{j=0}^{m−1} T_f(j/m,j/m).
Their sum divided by 3m+1 converges to ∫₀¹T_f(t,t)dt. This proves precisely the stated weak limit μ on X, with independent normalized angular Haar and Lebesgue dt of total mass one. Finally
m^(−1)B_m exp(−mw)ν=(N_m/m)μ_m→3μ,
whereas the positive measures normalized by m² have total mass N_m/m²→0 and hence converge weakly to zero. This proves the intrinsic, rather than ambient, normalization.

notes.summary: Complete identification using n1–n2: the full ideal envelope is P=g(x1+x2)-φ_X, where g(s)=0 (s≤0), s²/4 (0≤s≤2), s-1 (s≥2). The actual U_m have a global full-envelope lower bound and converge locally uniformly off the two poles, globally in L¹ at rate O(log m/m), pointwise as extended reals, and uniformly after exponentiation. A global additive uniform error is impossible because the actual pole coefficient is 1-1/m. Together with the exact spaces and normalized trace limit, this solves the stated task.
notes.detailedSummary: This fresh completion uses only fresh n1 and n2. For every possibly non-toric ideal competitor, pencil rigidity gives v=χ(z1z2)-φ_X. Its quasi-everywhere obstacle inequality is pointwise on the interior by genuine psh submean and zero volume of pluripolar exceptional sets. On equal radii this bounds χ by s²/4 for -2<s<4. The circle maximum of χ is finite convex with all slopes in [0,1]; testing a supporting line of slope p at s=2p gives the upper bound by g(s)=sup_{0≤p≤1}(ps-p²). The converse candidate is globally genuine θ-psh, ordinary and ideal, and lies below w; hence it is the full envelope. Diagonal elements of the actual three-band space yield U_m≥P+log(9m/(2π))/m-1/(4m²) globally. All three bands yield U_m≤P+[C+2log(m+1)+log R]/m, with R=1+min(e^{x1},e^{1-x2})+min(e^{x2},e^{1-x1}). R is bounded off the poles and at most C/r² near them. These give the stated convergence and a genuine uniform exponential topology, while the least actual vanishing order m-1 proves failure of any global additive uniform estimate. The probability trace limit is (14) in n2, and the full/ordinary envelope equality for every smooth global obstacle follows from n1.
notes.text:
This note completes the exact task using only the fresh notes n1 and n2. It does not use any dead note. The only non-elementary existence input in those notes is the precise weighted hyperplane-extension theorem recorded in n1; the hypotheses, weight convention, point corollary, and connectedness restrictions used here are all specified there.

1. THE FULL IDEAL ENVELOPE, INCLUDING NON-TORIC COMPETITORS.
Put φ_X(x)=log(1+e^{x1})+log(1+e^{x2}) and s=x1+x2. Define
 g(s)=sup_{0≤p≤1}(ps-p²)
 =0 for s≤0,
 =s²/4 for 0≤s≤2,
 =s-1 for s≥2.                                             (15)
The answer on the torus is
 P(x)=g(x1+x2)-φ_X(x).                                      (16)
It has the canonical global θ-psh extension described below, with value -∞ at the two fixed poles.

To prove the upper bound for the FULL competitor class, let v be any nontrivial ideal competitor. By n1 it has the possibly non-toric form
 v=χ(Q)-φ_X,  Q=z1z2,
where χ is subharmonic in the affine base coordinate and has upper growth χ(Q)≤max(0,log|Q|²)+C. The identically -∞ competitor needs no argument.

Let Ω be the interior of K, given by -1<x_i<2. The quasi-everywhere obstacle inequality implies an almost-everywhere inequality on Ω, since pluripolar sets have zero Euclidean volume. In the torus frame, the genuine psh local potential v+φ_X is therefore at most H=(x1²+x2²)/2 almost everywhere. Submean on balls contained in Ω, followed by shrinking them and using continuity of H, proves this inequality at every point of Ω. This step uses the canonical representative explicitly; it would be false for arbitrary artificially raised representatives of a curvature distribution.

For any base point with s=log|Q|²∈(-2,4), choose |z1|²=|z2|²=e^{s/2} and angles with product Q. The resulting point lies in Ω and gives
 χ(Q)≤s²/4.                                                (17)
Let c(s)=max_{|Q|²=e^s}χ(Q). It is finite and convex by the subharmonic three-circles theorem. It cannot be -∞ on an entire circle: upper semicontinuity would bound χ by arbitrarily negative constants in a neighborhood of that circle, and the maximum principle would make it identically -∞ inside and then on its connected domain. Its growth satisfies c(s)≤max(0,s)+C. Every supporting slope therefore lies in [0,1]: a negative slope contradicts the bound at -∞, and a slope greater than 1 contradicts the bound at +∞. Continuity of finite convex functions extends (17) to [-2,4].

For any real s, select p∈∂c(s). Since 2p∈[0,2], the supporting-line inequality and (17) give
 c(s)+p(2p-s)≤c(2p)≤p².
Thus c(s)≤ps-p²≤g(s), and χ(Q)≤g(log|Q|²). This proves v≤P on the torus without assuming angular invariance of v. Away from the poles, P is continuous, so the canonical submean property extends the inequality across the coordinate divisors. At the poles both v and P have value -∞.

Conversely, g is convex with slopes between 0 and 1. The function χ_g(Q)=g(log|Q|²) is subharmonic on C*, is constant near 0, and near ∞ differs from log|Q|² by the constant -1. It therefore gives an ω_FS-psh function
 u_g=χ_g-log(1+|Q|²)
on CP1. Use n1's pencil construction to extend (16) globally as a genuine θ-psh function. The elementary bounds
 -1≤g(s)-max(0,s)≤0
show ψ-1≤P≤ψ, so P belongs to the ordinary class and, by n1, the full ideal class. Finally
 g(s)≤s²/4≤(x1²+x2²)/2,
so P≤w pointwise on K. It is an admissible competitor, while every competitor is at most P. Hence the actual supremum, and its USC regularization, equal (16). Near each pole P=log r²+O(1), so the regularization also has value -∞ there. This proves the full ideal-envelope identification, not merely a toric-restricted one.

2. GLOBAL LOWER BOUND FROM THE ACTUAL SECTION SPACES.
Use the original norms and the complete three-band basis in n2. Its diagonal elements are among the actual selected elements, and (12) gives
 A_m(j,j)≤(2π/(9m))e^{j²/m}.
Consequently
 B_m≥(9m/(2π))e^{-mφ_X}max_{0≤j≤m}exp(js-j²/m).
For all real s,
 max_{0≤j≤m}[(j/m)s-(j/m)²]≥g(s)-1/(4m²):
for s≤0 and s≥2 the exact maximizing endpoint belongs to the grid; for 0≤s≤2 choose a nearest grid point to s/2 and lose at most its squared distance 1/(4m²). Therefore
 U_m≥P+log(9m/(2π))/m-1/(4m²).                             (18)
This is a global full-envelope lower bound on the torus. By continuity it extends to X minus the poles, and at a pole its right side is -∞. The correction tends to zero independently of the point.

Using diagonal elements for this lower bound does not replace the actual spaces by a diagonal subseries. Their dimensions, norms, measure limits, and the upper bound below concern all three bands. Indeed U_m itself is generally not an ideal/ordinary competitor: its pole coefficient is 1-1/m. Thus one cannot obtain the required upper bound by treating each U_m as admissible for the envelope.

3. UPPER BOUND FOR ALL THREE BANDS.
The lower norm bound (12) implies
 B_m≤(9m/c²)e^{-mφ_X}
       ∑_{0≤a,b≤m, |a-b|≤1}exp(a x1+b x2-(a²+b²)/(2m)).
Diagonal exponents are at most m g(s). For a=j+1,b=j, 0≤j≤m-1, comparison with diagonal index j gives an upper bound m g(s)+x1; comparison with index j+1 gives m g(s)+1-x2. Therefore the whole exponent is bounded by
 m g(s)+log min(e^{x1},e^{1-x2}).
The opposite band has the bound obtained by exchanging x1 and x2. Set
 R(x)=1+min(e^{x1},e^{1-x2})+min(e^{x2},e^{1-x1}).           (19)
Counting the terms gives
 B_m≤(9m(m+1)/c²)R(x)e^{mP(x)},
and hence, with a fixed constant C,
 U_m≤P+[C+2log(m+1)+log R(x)]/m.                            (20)
This uses every actual selected section.

The function R has a finite continuous extension across the coordinate divisors away from the poles and is bounded on each compact subset of X\{p,q}. For example at z1=0 with z2 finite its value is 1+|z2|², and at z1=∞ with z2 finite it is 1+e/|z2|². At (0,0) and (∞,∞) it is 1. Near p write u=z1, v=1/z2, A=|u|², B=|v|². Then
 R=1+min(A,eB)+min(1/B,e/A).
The first minimum is bounded and
 min(1/B,e/A)≤2e/(A+B).
Thus R≤C/r² for r²=|u|²+|v|² sufficiently small; the same estimate holds near q. In particular log R is integrable against every smooth volume form on X. Estimates (18) and (20) extend off the torus by continuity wherever both potentials are finite.

4. VALID CONVERGENCE TOPOLOGIES AND THE POLE LIMITATION.
The preceding bounds prove:
(a) U_m→P uniformly on every compact subset of X\{p,q}, with O(log m/m) error there. This includes coordinate-divisor points away from the poles, not just dense-torus compact sets.
(b) U_m→P globally in L¹ with respect to any smooth volume form, at rate O(log m/m), by integration of (18) and (20) and the integrability of log R. Values at the two points do not affect this assertion.
(c) U_m→P pointwise on all X as extended-real functions. At a pole, all selected sections vanish for m≥2, so U_m=-∞; P=-∞ also. For m=1 the actual space is all of H0(O(1,1)) and U_1 is finite there, which is immaterial to the limit.
(d) exp(U_m)→exp(P) uniformly on all X. To see this genuine global uniform statement, near a pole P≤log r²+C and R≤C/r². Estimate (20) gives, for m≥2,
 U_m≤(1-1/m)log r²+C+[C+2log(m+1)]/m.
The exponential is bounded by C r for r<1, uniformly in m≥2, while e^P≤Cr². These uniform smallness bounds near the poles, together with uniform convergence on their complement, establish (d).

There is NO global additive uniform error estimate for U_m-P. At p, the band b=a+1 consists locally of all degree-(m-1) binary monomials u^a v^{m-1-a}, 0≤a≤m-1, and all other selected sections have at least that order. Their positively weighted sum of squared leading forms is comparable to r^{2(m-1)} in every direction, with constants allowed to depend on m. The same holds at q using the opposite band. Thus, for fixed m≥2,
 U_m=(1-1/m)log r²+O_m(1),
 P=log r²+O(1).

 (3m+1)^{-1}B_m e^{-mw}ν,

reconstruction.statement:
Let X=CP¹×CP¹, L=O(1,1) with the product Fubini–Study metric h, θ=c₁(L,h), and dd^c=(i/(2π))∂∂̄. All θ-psh functions have genuine canonical psh local potentials. Let ψ=max(log|T₁T₂|²_h,log|Z₁Z₂|²_h), p=(0,∞), and q=(∞,0). On the dense torus write z_i=Z_i/T_i, x_i=log|z_i|², s=x₁+x₂, and φ_X=log(1+e^{x₁})+log(1+e^{x₂}). Let K consist of x∈[−1,2]² and all angles, set w=(x₁²+x₂²)/2−φ_X, and use ν=(1/9)dx₁dx₂ times independent normalized angular Haar. For each integer m≥1 use the entire actual space V_m=H⁰(X,L^m⊗I(mψ)), the norm ||s||²_m=∫_K|s|²_{h^m}e^(−mw)dν, its orthonormal kernel B_m, and U_m=m^(−1)log B_m.

Define
P_I=(sup{v:v is genuine θ-psh on X, I(tv)⊆I(tψ) for every real t>0, and v≤w quasi-everywhere on K})*.
Here * denotes USC regularization. Set
g(s)=sup_{0≤a≤1}(as−a²)=0 for s≤0, s²/4 for 0≤s≤2, and s−1 for s≥2.

1. The full ideal envelope is, on the dense torus,
P_I(x)=P(x):=g(x₁+x₂)−φ_X(x).
The function P has a canonical global θ-psh extension, is finite and continuous on X\{p,q}, and has P(p)=P(q)=−∞. Equivalently, off the base points it is ψ_FS+u_g∘F, where F=[T₁T₂:Z₁Z₂], ψ_FS=log(|T₁T₂|²_h+|Z₁Z₂|²_h), and u_g is the ω_FS-psh extension to CP¹ of g(log|Q|²)−log(1+|Q|²) on C*. Globally,
ψ−1≤P≤ψ,
and P≤w pointwise on K. Every genuine θ-psh competitor in the definition of P_I, including arbitrary non-toric competitors, satisfies v≤P on all of X. Thus the unregularized supremum also equals P. The full ideal class equals the ordinary class {v:v≤ψ+C_v for some finite C_v}; their envelopes consequently agree for every smooth real obstacle on all X as well.

2. For every integer m≥1 the actual kernels satisfy the global extended-real lower bound
U_m≥P+log(9m/(2π))/m−1/(4m²).
This bound uses the original Hilbert norm and applies to the full ideal envelope.

Let c=∫_{−1}¹e^(−y²/2)dy and, on the dense torus, define
R(x)=1+min(e^{x₁},e^{1−x₂})+min(e^{x₂},e^{1−x₁}).
For every integer m≥1,
B_m≤(9m(m+1)/c²)R e^(mP)
on X\{p,q}, with R extended continuously there. In particular, there is a finite constant C independent of m and the point such that
U_m≤P+[C+2log(m+1)+log R]/m
on X\{p,q}.

The extension of R is finite, continuous, and bounded on every compact subset of X\{p,q}. At z₁=0 with z₂ finite it equals 1+|z₂|²; at z₁=∞ with z₂ finite and nonzero it equals 1+e/|z₂|²; and at (0,0) and (∞,∞) it equals 1. Near p use (u,η)=(z₁,1/z₂), and near q use (u,η)=(1/z₁,z₂), with r²=|u|²+|η|². There is a finite constant C such that R≤C/r² near either pole. The function log R is integrable against every smooth volume form on X.

3. The actual kernel potentials have all of the following convergence properties:
(a) U_m→P uniformly on each compact subset E⊂X\{p,q}, with additive error O_E(log m/m). This includes points on coordinate divisors away from the poles.
(b) U_m→P in L¹(X,dV) for every smooth volume form dV, with ||U_m−P||_{L¹(dV)}=O_{dV}(log m/m); values at the two poles are immaterial to this assertion.
(c) U_m→P pointwise on all X as extended-real functions. At either pole, U_m=−∞ for every m≥2, while U₁ is finite.
(d) With e^(−∞)=0, e^{U_m}→e^P uniformly on all X. More specifically, in fixed sufficiently small neighborhoods of the two poles there is a constant C independent of m≥2 such that e^{U_m}≤Cr and e^P≤Cr².

For each fixed integer m≥2, near either pole and uniformly over approach directions,
U_m=(1−1/m)log r²+O_m(1),  P=log r²+O(1).
Thus U_m−P→+∞ on punctured approaches to either pole, and sup_{X\{p,q}}(U_m−P)=+∞. There is no global uniform additive error estimate for U_m−P. These finite-m kernel potentials are not themselves competitors in the full ideal or ordinary class: their pole coefficient is 1−1/m for m≥2, and U₁ is finite at the poles.

4. The entire actual spaces are
V_m=span{Z₁^aT₁^{m−a}Z₂^bT₂^{m−b}:0≤a,b≤m, |a−b|≤1},
with N_m=dim V_m=3m+1. Their intrinsic Hilbert growth dimension is 1 and N_m/m→3. For the original weighted Hilbert norm, the probability trace measures
(3m+1)^(−1)B_m e^(−mw)ν
converge weakly on X to the probability measure μ defined, for every continuous f on X, by
∫_X f dμ=∫₀¹∫₀^{2π}∫₀^{2π}f(z₁=e^{t/2+iθ₁},z₂=e^{t/2+iθ₂})dθ₁/(2π)dθ₂/(2π)dt.
This measure is supported on the contact set x₁=x₂=t, 0≤t≤1, where P=w. With intrinsic power normalization m^(−1) the weak limit is 3μ; with ambient normalization m^(−2) the weak limit is zero.
reconstruction.proof:
We use n1 and n2 in their proved forms. In particular, the arbitrary, non-toric ideal competitor class has already been identified in n1, and the spaces and norms used here are the entire actual ideal-selected spaces from n2. No convex-spectrum or general kernel convergence theorem is assumed.

1. Identification of the full envelope. Elementary maximization gives
sup_{0≤a≤1}(as−a²)=g(s),
with the three formulas in the statement. Its derivative is 0, then s/2, then 1. Thus g is convex and nondecreasing. The radial function χ_g(Q)=g(log|Q|²) is genuinely subharmonic on C*: the radial subharmonicity criterion is precisely nonnegative second derivative in log|Q|². The matching first derivatives at s=0,2 introduce no negative circle masses. It is identically zero near Q=0. At infinity, with ξ=1/Q, its other local potential is
χ_g(1/ξ)+log|ξ|²=−1
for |ξ| sufficiently small. It follows that u_g=χ_g−log(1+|Q|²) extends to a continuous genuine ω_FS-psh function on CP¹, taking values 0 at zero and −1 at infinity.

The representation result of n1 now gives a global θ-psh P=ψ_FS+u_g∘F, with the stated torus formula and canonical values −∞ at p,q. It is finite and continuous elsewhere. Directly from the formula for g,
max(0,s)−1≤g(s)≤max(0,s).
Thus ψ−1≤P≤ψ globally. Also g(s)≤s²/4 for every real s, while
H=(x₁²+x₂²)/2=s²/4+(x₁−x₂)²/4.
Consequently P≤w on K, pointwise. The ordinary bound P≤ψ implies its full ideal constraint by n1.

We prove the reverse envelope inequality for every competitor, without toricization. The identically −∞ competitor is harmless. For a nontrivial one, n1 supplies
v=χ(Q)−φ_X,  Q=z₁z₂,
where χ(Q)=log(1+|Q|²)+u(Q) is genuine subharmonic on C and u is genuine ω_FS-psh on CP¹. The quasi-everywhere obstacle bound is a pointwise bound in the interior of K. To see this, the exceptional pluripolar set has local Lebesgue measure zero, since a local nontrivial psh function is integrable. On any ball contained in the interior, the genuine local potential v+φ_X is therefore at most the continuous H almost everywhere. Its submean inequality followed by shrinking the ball gives v+φ_X≤H at the center.

For every s∈[0,2] and every Q of log|Q|²=s, choose x₁=x₂=s/2 and angles with product Q. These points lie in the interior of K. Hence
χ(Q)≤s²/4,  0≤s≤2.
On |Q|=1 this bound is zero. The subharmonic maximum principle on the unit disk, applicable also if χ has −∞ values, yields χ≤0 for |Q|≤1. For the other end, define the genuine subharmonic potential at infinity
χ_∞(ξ)=χ(1/ξ)+log|ξ|²=log(1+|ξ|²)+u(1/ξ).
On |ξ|=exp(−1) the preceding obstacle bound at s=2 gives χ_∞≤−1. The maximum principle on that disk gives χ_∞≤−1 inside, equivalently χ(Q)≤log|Q|²−1 when s≥2. Together these prove χ(Q)≤g(log|Q|²) for every Q∈C*, including angularly varying χ. Thus v≤P on the torus. Canonical local psh representatives and the same inequality almost everywhere extend it to the coordinate divisors away from the base points; at the base points both class members and P have value −∞ by n1. Therefore every competitor is at most P on all X.

Since P itself is a competitor, the unregularized supremum is exactly P. Its canonical global extension is USC, so the USC-regularized envelope is also P. Equality of the ordinary and full ideal classes, and their envelope equality for every smooth obstacle on all X, follow from n1, not from an assumption about toric competitors.

2. Exact lower bound and a global-away-from-poles upper bound. Let c be as in n2. Its original norm estimates give, for diagonal sections,
A_m(j,j)≤(2π/(9m))exp(j²/m).
Keeping only these actually selected sections in the actual kernel gives on the torus
B_m≥(9m/(2π))exp(−mφ_X) max_{0≤j≤m}exp(js−j²/m).
The continuous maximizer of as−a² on [0,1] is a*=min(1,max(0,s/2)). If it is an endpoint, the grid attains it exactly. Otherwise choose a grid point j/m within 1/(2m). The loss in the quadratic is at most 1/(4m²). Taking logarithms proves
U_m≥P+log(9m/(2π))/m−1/(4m²).
Exponentiating gives an inequality between continuous functions B_m and a constant times exp(mP), and extends it to every point of X. At p,q the extended-real inequality simply has right side −∞. Thus this is a global lower bound for the full ideal envelope, with the original Hilbert norm and all global section conditions accounted for.

For the upper bound, n2 gives
B_m≤(9m/c²)exp(−mφ_X)∑_{|a−b|≤1}exp(a x₁+b x₂−(a²+b²)/(2m)).
Each diagonal summand is at most exp(mg(s)). For a=j+1,b=j, 0≤j≤m−1, its exponent can be written in either of two ways:
js−j²/m+x₁−(2j+1)/(2m),
(j+1)s−(j+1)²/m−x₂+(2j+1)/(2m).
The first is at most mg(s)+x₁, and the second at most mg(s)+1−x₂. Thus the summand is bounded by exp(mg(s))min(exp x₁,exp(1−x₂)). Interchanging the two factors proves the analogous bound for a=b−1. There are m+1 diagonal terms and m on each adjacent diagonal, so
B_m≤(9m(m+1)/c²)R exp(mP),
with exactly the R in the statement. Taking logarithms, and using m(m+1)≤(m+1)², gives the asserted bound with a point-independent constant C.

Here are the required extension and integrability checks for R. On the torus it equals
1+min(|z₁|²,e/|z₂|²)+min(|z₂|²,e/|z₁|²).
This formula has a finite continuous extension wherever the two indeterminate pole configurations are avoided. At z₁=0 and finite z₂ its value is 1+|z₂|²; at z₁=∞ and finite nonzero z₂ it is 1+e/|z₂|². The symmetric formulas cover the other divisors, and the values at (0,0) and (∞,∞) are one. They also show local boundedness on compact subsets of X minus the poles.

Near p put A=|u|², B=|η|², r²=A+B. For r>0,
R=1+min(A,eB)+min(1/B,e/A),
with its natural continuous values on the axes. Since max(B,A/e)≥(A+B)/(e+1), the last term is at most (e+1)/r², while the middle term is at most e r². Hence R≤C/r² on a fixed small punctured neighborhood. The q calculation is the same with the variables interchanged. Since R≥1, these estimates imply 0≤log R≤C+|log r²| near each pole. The latter is integrable in four real dimensions against every smooth volume form. Thus log R is globally integrable. Continuity of B_m,P,R extends the upper inequality from the torus to X\{p,q}, but not through the poles as a finite additive estimate.

3. All convergence topologies and the necessary pole caveat. On a compact E⊂X\{p,q}, R is bounded. The lower and upper bounds just proved give
sup_E|U_m−P|=O_E(log m/m).
Both functions are finite there; the kernel is positive because the diagonal pencil sections have no common zero outside p,q. This proves (a), including the coordinate divisors.

Off the two poles the same inequalities give, with an absolute constant C,
|U_m−P|≤[C log(m+1)+log R]/m.
The preceding integrability result proves (b), with rate O_{dV}(log m/m) for any smooth volume form. Both potentials are locally integrable, and values at the two points play no role.

For m≥2 every selected section vanishes at both poles, so B_m(p)=B_m(q)=0 and U_m(p)=U_m(q)=−∞. At m=1 the entire O(1,1) space is selected and is base-point free, so U₁ is finite there. Since P has value −∞ there and convergence elsewhere was proved above, this gives extended-real pointwise convergence on all X, as in (c).

For (d), note that exp(U_m)=B_m^(1/m) is continuous everywhere and exp(P) is continuous, also at the poles. Near either pole the comparison with ψ gives exp(P)≤C₀r². The upper bound yields
exp(U_m)≤[9m(m+1)/c²]^(1/m) R^(1/m)exp(P)
≤C r^(2−2/m),  m≥2,
where C is independent of m: the displayed numerical prefactors and the powers of the fixed R-bound constant are bounded for m≥2. For r≤1, r^(2−2/m)≤r. Thus exp(U_m)≤Cr and exp(P)≤Cr² in fixed sufficiently small pole neighborhoods. Make those neighborhoods small, and then use uniform convergence on their compact complement to obtain uniform convergence exp(U_m)→exp(P) on all X.

We also verify precisely why additive uniform convergence fails. Near p the sections on the adjacent diagonal b=a+1, a=0,…,m−1, have local coefficients
u^aη^(m−1−a).
These are all homogeneous monomials of degree m−1. Their squared absolute values, with the positive fixed norm coefficients, bound B_m from below by c_m r^(2(m−1)) uniformly in direction. Every other selected coefficient has order at least m−1, which gives an upper bound C_m r^(2(m−1)) on a fixed small ball. The metric factor is smooth and bounded above and below there. The same argument at q uses a=b+1. Therefore, for fixed m≥2,
U_m=(1−1/m)log r²+O_m(1)
uniformly over approach directions. The comparison ψ−1≤P≤ψ gives P=log r²+O(1), also uniformly. Consequently
U_m−P=−(1/m)log r²+O_m(1)→+∞
on punctured approaches to either pole. In particular its supremum on X\{p,q} is infinite for every fixed m≥2. There is no uniform additive global boundary error estimate. The finite-m kernel potentials are genuine θ-psh, but are not ordinary competitors: for m≥2 their coefficient 1−1/m is too small, and U₁ is finite at the poles. By n1 they are not full ideal competitors either. The envelope lower convergence proved above does not depend on incorrectly treating them as competitors.

4. Intrinsic normalization and measure. By n2 the complete spaces are exactly the stated three-diagonal spaces, N_m=3m+1, with intrinsic Hilbert growth dimension one. That note proves directly from the original norms that
(3m+1)^(−1)B_m exp(−mw)ν⇀μ,
where μ is exactly dt on x₁=x₂=t∈[0,1] times independent normalized angular Haar, with the displayed integral formula for every continuous f on X. No ambient-dimensional trace normalization enters this calculation. The intrinsic normalization by m therefore gives 3μ, whereas normalization by m² gives zero.

Finally, on K,
w−P=(x₁−x₂)²/4+[s²/4−g(s)].
Both summands are nonnegative. The second vanishes precisely for s∈[0,2]; outside that interval it equals s²/4 for s<0 and (s−2)²/4 for s>2. Thus the contact set is exactly x₁=x₂=t with 0≤t≤1, with all angles. This confirms the claimed support and completes the entire envelope, potential, and kernel-measure identification.

premises: Weighted point L² extension, in the point form of the Ohsawa–Takegoshi theorem: Let B be a bounded Euclidean ball in C^n and B' a smaller concentric ball with closure contained in B. There is a constant C depending only on B, B', and n such that, for every plurisubharmonic function Φ on B and every a in B' with Φ(a)>−∞, there is F holomorphic on B satisfying F(a)=1 and ∫_B |F|² exp(−Φ) dV ≤ C exp(−Φ(a)). The constant is independent of Φ and a, and singular plurisubharmonic weights are permitted. The weight convention is exp(−Φ).

Plurisubharmonic radial three-circles theorem: If φ is a non-identically−∞ plurisubharmonic function on B(0,R) in C^n, then M(s)=sup_{|z|≤exp(s/2)} φ(z) is finite, nondecreasing, and convex for s<2 log R.

Restriction and uniqueness properties of canonical plurisubharmonic functions: If φ is plurisubharmonic on a complex manifold and G is a holomorphic map from a connected complex manifold into its domain, then φ∘G is plurisubharmonic or identically −∞. A non-identically−∞ plurisubharmonic function is locally integrable, and two canonical plurisubharmonic functions that agree almost everywhere agree everywhere.

Removable extension for plurisubharmonic functions: Let A be a proper analytic subset of a complex manifold Ω. If φ is plurisubharmonic on Ω\A and locally bounded above near A, its canonical upper extension, defined at A by the limit superior from Ω\A, is plurisubharmonic on Ω.
